##### Exposition of Results Rooted in the Unwholesome ^2-6-2-15-0

350. Which states are neutral? At the time when, as a result of unwholesome action having been done and accumulated, a resultant eye-consciousness has arisen, accompanied by equanimity, having a sight as its object — at that time, dependent on an unwholesome root, a formation comes to be. Dependent on the formation, consciousness comes to be. Dependent on consciousness, mentality comes to be. Dependent on mentality, the sixth sense-field comes to be. Dependent on the sixth sense-field, contact comes to be. Dependent on contact, feeling comes to be. Dependent on feeling, existence comes to be. Dependent on existence, birth comes to be. Dependent on birth, aging-and-death comes to be. Thus does this entire mass of suffering come to be. ^2-350

351. Herein, what is the formation dependent on an unwholesome root? Whatever is volition, intention, the state of intending: this is called "the formation dependent on an unwholesome root" ... That is why it is said, "thus does this entire mass of suffering come to be." ^2-351

352. Which states are neutral? At the time when, as a result of unwholesome action having been done and accumulated, a resultant ear-consciousness has arisen, accompanied by equanimity, having a sound as its object ... or a resultant nose-consciousness has arisen, accompanied by equanimity, having a smell as its object ... or a resultant tongue-consciousness has arisen, accompanied by equanimity, having a taste as its object ... or a resultant body-consciousness has arisen, accompanied by pain, having a tangible object as its object ... or a resultant mind element has arisen, accompanied by equanimity, having as its object a sight ... or a tangible object, or whatever else it may be about — at that time, dependent on an unwholesome root, a formation comes to be. Dependent on the formation, consciousness comes to be. Dependent on consciousness, mentality comes to be. Dependent on mentality, the sixth sense-field comes to be. Dependent on the sixth sense-field, contact comes to be. Dependent on contact, feeling comes to be. Dependent on feeling, resolve comes to be. Dependent on resolve, existence comes to be. Dependent on existence, birth comes to be. Dependent on birth, aging-and-death comes to be. Thus does this entire mass of suffering come to be. ^2-352

353. Which states are neutral? At the time when, as a result of unwholesome action having been done and accumulated, a resultant mind-consciousness element has arisen, accompanied by equanimity, having as its object a sight ... or a mental object, or whatever else it may be about — at that time, dependent on an unwholesome root, a formation comes to be. Dependent on the formation, consciousness comes to be. Dependent on consciousness, mentality comes to be. Dependent on mentality, the sixth sense-field comes to be. Dependent on the sixth sense-field, contact comes to be. Dependent on contact, feeling comes to be. Dependent on feeling, resolve comes to be. Dependent on resolve, existence comes to be. Dependent on existence, birth comes to be. Dependent on birth, aging-and-death comes to be. Thus does this entire mass of suffering come to be. ^2-353

354. Herein, what is the formation dependent on an unwholesome root? Whatever is volition, intention, the state of intending: this is called "the formation dependent on an unwholesome root".
Herein, what is the consciousness dependent on the formation? Whatever is mind, mentality ... the corresponding mind-consciousness element: this is called "the consciousness dependent on the formation".
Herein, what is the mentality dependent on consciousness? The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations: this is called "the mentality dependent on consciousness".
Herein, what is the sixth sense-field dependent on mentality? Whatever is mind, mentality ... the corresponding mind-consciousness element: this is called "the sixth sense-field dependent on mentality".
Herein, what is the contact dependent on the sixth sense-field? Whatever is contact, touching, the act of touching, the state of touching: this is called "the contact dependent on the sixth sense-field".
Herein, what is the feeling dependent on contact? Whatever is neither mental comfort nor mental discomfort, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of mental contact, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that is felt and is born of mental contact: this is called "the feeling dependent on contact".
Herein, what is the resolve dependent on feeling? Whatever is the mind's resolve, resolving, the state of being resolved: this is called "the resolve dependent on feeling".
Herein, what is the existence dependent on resolve? Apart from resolve, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, the aggregate of consciousness: this is called "the existence dependent on resolve".
Herein, what is the birth dependent on existence? Whatever, of those various states, is birth, coming to birth, production, coming into being, appearance: this is called "the birth dependent on existence".
Herein, what is the aging-and-death dependent on birth? There is aging, and there is death. Herein, what is aging? Whatever, of those various states, is aging, decrepitude, the decline of the lifespan: this is called "aging". Herein, what is death? Whatever, of those various states, is destruction, decay, breaking up, disintegration, impermanence, disappearance: this is called "death". Thus there is this aging, and this death. This is called "the aging-and-death dependent on birth".
That "thus does this entire mass of suffering come to be" means: thus does this entire mass of suffering come together, meet, unite, and appear. That is why it is said, "thus does this entire mass of suffering come to be."
Exposition of Results Rooted in the Unwholesome.
Abhidhamma Classification.
The Analysis of Dependent Origination is finished. ^2-354

### Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness ^2-7-0

#### Discourse Classification ^2-7-1-0

355. The four foundations of mindfulness: here a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, dwells contemplating the body in the body externally, dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; dwells contemplating feelings in feelings internally, dwells contemplating feelings in feelings externally, dwells contemplating feelings in feelings both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; dwells contemplating the mind in the mind internally, dwells contemplating the mind in the mind externally, dwells contemplating the mind in the mind both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; dwells contemplating mental objects in mental objects internally, dwells contemplating mental objects in mental objects externally, dwells contemplating mental objects in mental objects both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. ^2-355

##### Exposition of Contemplation of the Body ^2-7-1-1-0

356. How does a monk dwell internally contemplating the body in the body? Here a monk reviews this very body, from the soles of the feet up and from the hair of the head down, enclosed by skin, full of many kinds of impurities: "In this body there are head-hair, body-hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, membranes, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, oil of the joints, and urine." He practises that sign, develops it, cultivates it, and establishes it well. Having practised that sign, developed it, cultivated it, and established it well, he directs his mind to the body externally.
How does a monk dwell externally contemplating the body in the body? Here a monk reviews another's body, from the soles of the feet up and from the hair of the head down, enclosed by skin, full of many kinds of impurities: "In his body there are head-hair, body-hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, membranes, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, oil of the joints, and urine." He practises that sign, develops it, cultivates it, and establishes it well. Having practised that sign, developed it, cultivated it, and established it well, he directs his mind to the body both internally and externally.
How does a monk dwell both internally and externally contemplating the body in the body? Here a monk reviews this body, from the soles of the feet up and from the hair of the head down, enclosed by skin, full of many kinds of impurities: "In this body there are head-hair, body-hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, membranes, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, oil of the joints, and urine." In this way a monk dwells both internally and externally contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. ^2-356

357. As to "one who contemplates": herein, what is contemplation? The wisdom, understanding... non-delusion, investigation of states, right view: this is called "contemplation". One who has this contemplation is endowed with it, fully endowed with it, has arrived at it, has fully arrived at it, has attained it, has fully attained it, and possesses it. Therefore it is called "one who contemplates". ^2-357

358. As to "dwells": he behaves, conducts himself, maintains himself, keeps himself going, carries on, lives, dwells. Therefore it is called "dwells". ^2-358

359. As to "ardent": herein, what is ardor? Whatever mental arousing of energy... right effort: this is called "ardor". One who has this ardor is endowed with it, fully endowed with it, has arrived at it, has fully arrived at it, has attained it, has fully attained it, and possesses it. Therefore it is called "ardent". ^2-359

360. As to "clearly comprehending": herein, what is clear comprehension? The wisdom, understanding... non-delusion, investigation of states, right view: this is called "clear comprehension". One who has this clear comprehension is endowed with it, fully endowed with it, has arrived at it, has fully arrived at it, has attained it, has fully attained it, and possesses it. Therefore it is called "clearly comprehending". ^2-360

361. As to "mindful": herein, what is mindfulness? Whatever mindfulness, recollection... right mindfulness: this is called "mindfulness". One who has this mindfulness is endowed with it, fully endowed with it, has arrived at it, has fully arrived at it, has attained it, has fully attained it, and possesses it. Therefore it is called "mindful". ^2-361

362. As to "having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world": herein, what is the world? That very body is the world. The five aggregates subject to clinging are the world. This is called "the world". Herein, what is covetousness? Whatever lust, passion... the mind's passion: this is called "covetousness". Herein, what is displeasure? Whatever mental discomfort, mental pain, the unpleasant, painful feeling born of mental contact, the unpleasant, painful feeling that is felt and is born of mental contact: this is called "displeasure". Thus this covetousness and this displeasure, in regard to this world, are removed, thoroughly removed, calmed, stilled, settled, ended, fully ended, quenched, extinguished, dried up, thoroughly dried up, and brought to an end. Therefore it is called "having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world".
Exposition of Contemplation of the Body. ^2-362

##### Exposition of Contemplation of Feeling ^2-7-1-2-0

363. How does a monk dwell internally contemplating feelings in feelings? Here, feeling a pleasant feeling, a monk knows, "I feel a pleasant feeling"; feeling a painful feeling, he knows, "I feel a painful feeling"; feeling a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows, "I feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling"; feeling a worldly pleasant feeling, he knows, "I feel a worldly pleasant feeling"; feeling an unworldly pleasant feeling, he knows, "I feel an unworldly pleasant feeling"; feeling a worldly painful feeling, he knows, "I feel a worldly painful feeling"; feeling an unworldly painful feeling, he knows, "I feel an unworldly painful feeling"; feeling a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows, "I feel a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling"; feeling an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows, "I feel an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling". He practises that sign, develops it, cultivates it, and establishes it well. Having practised that sign, developed it, cultivated it, and established it well, he directs his mind to feelings externally.
How does a monk dwell externally contemplating feelings in feelings? Here, of one feeling a pleasant feeling, he knows, "he feels a pleasant feeling"; of one feeling a painful feeling, he knows, "he feels a painful feeling"; of one feeling a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows, "he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling"; of one feeling a worldly pleasant feeling, he knows, "he feels a worldly pleasant feeling"; of one feeling an unworldly pleasant feeling, he knows, "he feels an unworldly pleasant feeling"; of one feeling a worldly painful feeling, he knows, "he feels a worldly painful feeling"; of one feeling an unworldly painful feeling, he knows, "he feels an unworldly painful feeling"; of one feeling a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows, "he feels a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling"; of one feeling an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows, "he feels an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling". ##### Exposition of Contemplation of the Mind ^2-7-1-3-0

365. How does a monk dwell internally contemplating the mind in the mind? Here, a monk knows a mind with lust as "my mind has lust"; he knows a mind without lust as "my mind is without lust"; he knows a mind with hate as "my mind has hate"; he knows a mind without hate as "my mind is without hate"; he knows a mind with delusion as "my mind has delusion"; he knows a mind without delusion as "my mind is without delusion"; he knows a contracted mind as "my mind is contracted"; he knows a distracted mind as "my mind is distracted"; he knows an expanded mind as "my mind is expanded"; he knows an unexpanded mind as "my mind is unexpanded"; he knows a surpassable mind as "my mind is surpassable"; he knows an unsurpassable mind as "my mind is unsurpassable"; he knows a concentrated mind as "my mind is concentrated"; he knows an unconcentrated mind as "my mind is unconcentrated"; he knows a freed mind as "my mind is freed"; he knows an unfreed mind as "my mind is unfreed". Having practised that sign, developed it, cultivated it, and established it well, he directs his mind to the mind externally.

##### Exposition of Contemplation of Mental Objects ^2-7-1-4-0

367. How does a monk dwell internally contemplating mental objects in mental objects? Here, when sense-desire is present within him, a monk knows, "I have sense-desire within me"; when sense-desire is absent, he knows, "I have no sense-desire within me"; and he knows how unarisen sense-desire comes to arise, how arisen sense-desire is abandoned, and how abandoned sense-desire does not arise again in the future. When ill-will is present within him... when dullness and drowsiness are present within him... when restlessness and remorse are present within him... when doubt is present within him, he knows, "I have doubt within me"; when doubt is absent, he knows, "I have no doubt within me"; and he knows how unarisen doubt comes to arise, how arisen doubt is abandoned, and how abandoned doubt does not arise again in the future.
When the awakening factor of mindfulness is present within him, he knows, "I have the awakening factor of mindfulness within me"; when it is absent, he knows, "I have no awakening factor of mindfulness within me"; and he knows how the unarisen awakening factor of mindfulness comes to arise, and how the arisen awakening factor of mindfulness is fulfilled by development. When the awakening factor of investigation of states is present within him... when the awakening factor of energy is present within him... when the awakening factor of joy is present within him... when the awakening factor of tranquility is present within him... when the awakening factor of concentration is present within him... when the awakening factor of equanimity is present within him, he knows, "I have the awakening factor of equanimity within me"; when it is absent, he knows, "I have no awakening factor of equanimity within me"; and he knows how the unarisen awakening factor of equanimity comes to arise, and how the arisen awakening factor of equanimity is fulfilled by development. He practises that sign, develops it, cultivates it, and establishes it well. Having practised that sign, developed it, cultivated it, and established it well, he directs his mind to mental objects externally.
How does a monk dwell externally contemplating mental objects in mental objects? Here, when sense-desire is present in him, a monk knows, "he has sense-desire in him"; when sense-desire is absent, he knows, "he has no sense-desire in him"; and he knows how unarisen sense-desire comes to arise, how arisen sense-desire is abandoned, and how abandoned sense-desire does not arise again in the future. When ill-will is present in him... when dullness and drowsiness are present in him... when restlessness and remorse are present in him... when doubt is present in him, he knows, "he has doubt in him"; when doubt is absent, he knows, "he has no doubt in him"; and he knows how unarisen doubt comes to arise, how arisen doubt is abandoned, and how abandoned doubt does not arise again in the future.
When the awakening factor of mindfulness is present in him, he knows, "he has the awakening factor of mindfulness in him"; when it is absent, he knows, "he has no awakening factor of mindfulness in him"; and he knows how the unarisen awakening factor of mindfulness comes to arise, and how the arisen awakening factor of mindfulness is fulfilled by development. When the awakening factor of investigation of states is present in him... when the awakening factor of energy is present in him... when the awakening factor of joy is present in him... when the awakening factor of tranquility is present in him... when the awakening factor of concentration is present in him... when the awakening factor of equanimity is present in him, he knows, "he has the awakening factor of equanimity in him"; when it is absent, he knows, "he has no awakening factor of equanimity in him"; and he knows how the unarisen awakening factor of equanimity comes to arise, and how the arisen awakening factor of equanimity is fulfilled by development. He practises that sign, develops it, cultivates it, and establishes it well. Having practised that sign, developed it, cultivated it, and established it well, he directs his mind to mental objects both internally and externally.
How does a monk dwell both internally and externally contemplating mental objects in mental objects? Here, when sense-desire is present, a monk knows, "there is sense-desire"; when sense-desire is absent, he knows, "there is no sense-desire"; and he knows how unarisen sense-desire comes to arise, how arisen sense-desire is abandoned, and how abandoned sense-desire does not arise again in the future. When ill-will is present... when dullness and drowsiness are present... when restlessness and remorse are present... when doubt is present, he knows, "there is doubt"; when doubt is absent, he knows, "there is no doubt"; and he knows how unarisen doubt comes to arise, how arisen doubt is abandoned, and how abandoned doubt does not arise again in the future.
When the awakening factor of mindfulness is present, he knows, "there is the awakening factor of mindfulness"; when it is absent, he knows, "there is no awakening factor of mindfulness"; and he knows how the unarisen awakening factor of mindfulness comes to arise, and how the arisen awakening factor of mindfulness is fulfilled by development. When the awakening factor of investigation of states is present... when the awakening factor of energy is present... when the awakening factor of joy is present... when the awakening factor of tranquility is present... when the awakening factor of concentration is present... when the awakening factor of equanimity is present, he knows, "there is the awakening factor of equanimity"; when it is absent, he knows, "there is no awakening factor of equanimity"; and he knows how the unarisen awakening factor of equanimity comes to arise, and how the arisen awakening factor of equanimity is fulfilled by development. In this way a monk dwells both internally and externally contemplating mental objects in mental objects, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. ^2-367

368. As to "one who contemplates": herein, what is contemplation? The wisdom, understanding... non-delusion, investigation of states, right view: this is called "contemplation". One who has this contemplation is endowed with it, fully endowed with it, has arrived at it, has fully arrived at it, has attained it, has fully attained it, and possesses it. Therefore it is called "one who contemplates". ^2-368

369. As to "dwells": he behaves, conducts himself, maintains himself, keeps himself going, carries on, lives, dwells. Therefore it is called "dwells". ^2-369

370. As to "ardent": herein, what is ardor? Whatever mental arousing of energy... right effort: this is called "ardor". One who has this ardor is endowed with it... possesses it. Therefore it is called "ardent". ^2-370

371. As to "clearly comprehending": herein, what is clear comprehension? The wisdom, understanding... non-delusion, investigation of states, right view: this is called "clear comprehension". One who has this clear comprehension is endowed with it... possesses it. Therefore it is called "clearly comprehending". ^2-371

372. As to "mindful": herein, what is mindfulness? Whatever mindfulness, recollection... right mindfulness: this is called "mindfulness". One who has this mindfulness is endowed with it... possesses it. Therefore it is called "mindful". ^2-372

373. As to "having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world": herein, what is the world? Those very mental objects are the world. The five aggregates subject to clinging are the world. This is called "the world". Herein, what is covetousness? Whatever lust, passion... the mind's passion: this is called "covetousness". Herein, what is displeasure? Whatever mental discomfort, mental pain, the unpleasant, painful feeling born of mental contact, the unpleasant, painful feeling that is felt and is born of mental contact: this is called "displeasure". Thus this covetousness and this displeasure, in regard to this world, are removed, thoroughly removed, calmed, stilled, settled, ended, fully ended, quenched, extinguished, dried up, thoroughly dried up, and brought to an end. Therefore it is called "having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world".
Exposition of Contemplation of Mental Objects.
Discourse Classification. ^2-373

#### Abhidhamma Classification ^2-7-2-0

374. The four foundations of mindfulness: here a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, dwells contemplating mental objects in mental objects. ^2-374

375. How does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body? Here, at the time when a monk develops the world-transcending absorption that leads out of the world and leads to the dismantling of accumulation, for the abandoning of wrong views and for reaching the first stage — quite secluded from sense pleasures... he enters and dwells in the first absorption, a difficult practice with slow direct knowledge, contemplating the body in the body — the mindfulness that is present on that occasion, the recollection, right mindfulness, the awakening factor of mindfulness, a path factor, included in the path: this is called "the foundation of mindfulness". The remaining states are joined with the foundation of mindfulness. ^2-375

#### Questions and Answers ^2-7-3-0

386. The four foundations of mindfulness: here a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; dwells contemplating mental objects in mental objects, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. ^2-386

387. Of the four foundations of mindfulness, how many are wholesome, how many unwholesome, how many neutral... how many conflicted, how many peaceful? ^2-387

##### Triads ^2-7-3-1-0

388. They may be wholesome, or may be neutral. They may be joined with pleasant feeling, or may be joined with neutral feeling. They may be a result, or may produce a result. They are not clung to but able to be clung to. They are not defiled but open to defilement. They may have applied and sustained thought, may have only sustained thought, or may have neither. They may be accompanied by joy, may be accompanied by happiness, or may be accompanied by equanimity. They are to be abandoned by neither seeing nor development. They are rooted in neither what is to be abandoned by seeing nor what is to be abandoned by development. They may lead to dismantling, or may lead to neither. They may be still in training, or may be beyond training. They are measureless. They have a measureless object. They are superior. They may be fixed in rightness, or may be not fixed. They do not have the path as object, but may have the path as root, may have the path as dominant factor, or should not be said to have the path as root or as dominant factor. They may be arisen, may be not arisen, or may be bound to arise. They may be past, may be future, or may be present. They should not be said to have a past object, a future object, or a present object. They may be internal, may be external, or may be both internal and external. They have an external object. They are invisible and without resistance. ^2-388

##### Pairs ^2-7-3-2-0

389. They are not a root. They are rooted. They are joined with a root. They should not be said to be both a root and rooted; they are rooted but not themselves a root. They should not be said to be both a root and joined with a root; they are joined with a root but not themselves a root. They are not a root, but are rooted.
They have conditions. They are conditioned. They are invisible. They offer no resistance. They are immaterial. They are beyond the world. They are knowable by some kinds of consciousness, not knowable by others. They are not themselves a mental taint. They are free of mental taints. They are dissociated from a mental taint. They should not be said to be both a mental taint and subject to mental taints, or to be subject to mental taints but not itself a mental taint. They should not be said to be both a mental taint and joined with a mental taint, or to be joined with a mental taint but not itself a mental taint. They are dissociated from a mental taint and free of it. They are not themselves a fetter... not themselves a tie... not themselves a flood... not themselves a yoke... not themselves a hindrance... not themselves wrong grasping... They have an object. They are not mind. They are mental factors. They are joined with mind. They are mingled with mind. They originate from mind. They co-arise with mind. They follow mind. They are mingled with mind and originating from mind. They are mingled with mind, originating from mind, and co-arising with mind. They are mingled with mind, originating from mind, and following mind. They are external. They are not derived. They are not clung to. They are not themselves clinging... not themselves a defilement... They are not to be abandoned by seeing, and not to be abandoned by development. They are not rooted in what is to be abandoned by seeing. They are not rooted in what is to be abandoned by development.
They may have applied thought, or may lack applied thought. They may have sustained thought, or may lack sustained thought. They may have joy, or may lack joy. They may be accompanied by joy, or may not be accompanied by joy. They may be accompanied by happiness, or may not be accompanied by happiness. They may be accompanied by equanimity, or may not be accompanied by equanimity. They do not belong to the sense sphere. They do not belong to the fine-material sphere. They do not belong to the immaterial sphere. They are unincluded. They may lead to liberation, or may not lead to liberation. They may be fixed, or may not be fixed. They are unsurpassed. They are peaceful.
Questions and Answers.
The Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness is finished. ^2-389

390. The four right efforts: here a monk, for the non-arising of unarisen bad, unwholesome states, generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives; for the abandoning of arisen bad, unwholesome states, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives; for the arising of unarisen wholesome states, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives; for the continuation, non-confusion, increase, expansion, and fulfilment by development of arisen wholesome states, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives. ^2-390

391. How does a monk, for the non-arising of unarisen bad, unwholesome states, generate desire, make an effort, arouse energy, exert the mind, and strive? Herein, what are unarisen bad, unwholesome states? The three unwholesome roots — greed, hatred, delusion — and the defilements bound up with them; the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness joined with them; and the bodily action, verbal action, and mental action that originate from them: these are called "unarisen bad, unwholesome states". Thus, for the non-arising of these unarisen bad, unwholesome states, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives. ^2-391

392. As to "generates desire": herein, what is desire? Whatever desire, state of desiring, wish to act, wholesome desire for the teaching: this is called "desire". He produces this desire, generates it, sets it going, sets it in motion, brings it forth, and brings it fully forth. Therefore it is called "generates desire". ^2-392

393. As to "makes an effort": herein, what is effort? Whatever mental exertion of energy... right effort: this is called "effort". One who has this effort is endowed with it, fully endowed with it, has arrived at it, has fully arrived at it, has attained it, has fully attained it, and possesses it. Therefore it is called "makes an effort". ^2-393

394. As to "arouses energy": herein, what is energy? Whatever mental exertion of energy... right effort: this is called "energy". He rouses this energy, thoroughly rouses it, practises it, develops it, and cultivates it. Therefore it is called "arouses energy". ^2-394

##### Triads ^2-8-3-1-0

429. They are only wholesome. They may be joined with pleasant feeling, or may be joined with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. They are things that produce a result. They are not clung to and not able to be clung to. They are not defiled and not open to defilement. They may have applied and sustained thought, may have only sustained thought, or may have neither. They have a measureless object. They are superior. They are fixed in rightness. They do not have the path as object. They have the path as root. They may have the path as dominant factor, or should not be said to have the path as dominant factor. They may be arisen, or may be not arisen; they should not be said to be bound to arise. They may be past, may be future, or may be present. They should not be said to have a past object, a future object, or a present object. ### Analysis of the Bases of Power ^2-9-0

431. The four bases of success: here a monk develops the basis of success endowed with concentration through desire and formation of endeavour; he develops the basis of success endowed with concentration through energy and formation of endeavour; he develops the basis of success endowed with concentration through mind and formation of endeavour; he develops the basis of success endowed with concentration through investigation and formation of endeavour. ^2-431

##### Base of Power through Desire ^2-9-1-1-0

432. How does a monk develop the basis of success endowed with concentration through desire and formation of endeavour? If a monk, having made desire the dominant factor, gains concentration, gains one-pointedness of mind — this is called "concentration through desire". For the non-arising of unarisen bad, unwholesome states, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives; for the abandoning of arisen bad, unwholesome states, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives; for the arising of unarisen wholesome states, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives; for the continuation, non-confusion, increase, expansion, and fulfilment by development of arisen wholesome states, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives. These are called "the formations of endeavour". Thus this concentration through desire, and these formations of endeavour — having combined and condensed them together, they are reckoned as "concentration through desire and formation of endeavour". ^2-432

433. Herein, what is desire? Whatever desire, state of desiring, wish to act, wholesome desire for the teaching: this is called "desire".
Herein, what is concentration? Whatever steadiness of mind, its stability, steadfastness, non-distraction, non-wavering, an undistracted state of mind, calm, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, right concentration: this is called "concentration".
Herein, what is the formation of endeavour? Whatever mental arousing of energy, launching out, exertion, endeavoring, striving, zeal, vigor, steadfastness, persistence without slackening, not giving up the desire to act, not putting down the task, taking up the task, energy, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, right effort: this is called "the formation of endeavour". Thus he is endowed with this desire, this concentration, and this formation of endeavour, fully endowed with it, has arrived at it, has fully arrived at it, has attained it, has fully attained it, and possesses it. Therefore it is called "endowed with concentration through desire and formation of endeavour". ^2-433

434. As to "power": whatever is the power, achievement, succeeding, prospering, obtaining, gaining, attainment, accomplishment, touching, realizing, and full attainment of those states.
As to "the basis of success": for one who has become thus, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
As to "develops the basis of success": he practises these states, develops them, and cultivates them. Therefore it is called "develops the basis of success". ^2-434

The basis of success through investigation is both a root and joined with a root; the other three bases of success should not be said to be both a root and joined with a root — they are joined with a root but not themselves a root. They should not be said to be both a mental taint and joined with a mental taint, or to be joined with a mental taint but not itself a mental taint. They are dissociated from a mental taint and free of it.

The other three bases of success are mingled with mind and originating from mind; the basis of success through mind is not mingled with mind and originating from mind. The other three bases of success are mingled with mind, originating from mind, and following mind; the basis of success through mind is not mingled with mind, originating from mind, and following mind.

### Analysis of the Awakening Factors ^2-10-0

#### Discourse Classification ^2-10-1-0

466. The seven awakening factors: the factor of mindfulness, the factor of investigation, the factor of energy, the factor of joy, the factor of tranquillity, the factor of concentration, the factor of equanimity. ^2-466

467. Herein, what is the factor of mindfulness? Here a monk is mindful, endowed with the highest mindfulness and alertness, able to recall and remember what was done and said long ago — this is called "the factor of mindfulness".
Dwelling thus mindfully, he investigates that state with wisdom, examines it, and inquires into it thoroughly — this is called "the factor of investigation".
As he investigates, examines, and inquires thoroughly into that state with wisdom, tireless energy arises in him — this is called "the factor of energy".
For one whose energy is aroused, unworldly joy arises — this is called "the factor of joy".
For one who is joyful in mind, the body becomes tranquil, and the mind also becomes tranquil — this is called "the factor of tranquillity".
For one whose body is tranquil and who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated — this is called "the factor of concentration".
Dwelling thus with mind concentrated, he looks on well with equanimity — this is called "the factor of equanimity". ^2-467

468. The seven awakening factors: the factor of mindfulness, the factor of investigation, the factor of energy, the factor of joy, the factor of tranquillity, the factor of concentration, the factor of equanimity. ^2-468

469. Herein, what is the factor of mindfulness? There is mindfulness of internal things, and there is mindfulness of external things. Whichever mindfulness of internal things there is, that factor of mindfulness leads to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna. Whichever mindfulness of external things there is, that factor of mindfulness leads to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna.
Herein, what is the factor of investigation? There is examination of internal things, and there is examination of external things. Whichever examination of internal things there is, that factor of investigation leads to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna. Whichever examination of external things there is, that factor of investigation leads to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna.
Herein, what is the factor of energy? There is bodily energy, and there is mental energy. Whichever bodily energy there is, that factor of energy leads to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna. Whichever mental energy there is, that factor of energy leads to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna.
Herein, what is the factor of joy? There is joy accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and there is joy without applied and sustained thought. Whichever joy accompanied by applied and sustained thought there is, that factor of joy leads to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna. Whichever joy without applied and sustained thought there is, that factor of joy leads to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna.
Herein, what is the factor of tranquillity? There is tranquillity of body, and there is tranquillity of mind. Whichever tranquillity of body there is, that factor of tranquillity leads to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna. Whichever tranquillity of mind there is, that factor of tranquillity leads to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna.
Herein, what is the factor of concentration? There is concentration accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and there is concentration without applied and sustained thought. Whichever concentration accompanied by applied and sustained thought there is, that factor of concentration leads to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna. Whichever concentration without applied and sustained thought there is, that factor of concentration leads to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna.
Herein, what is the factor of equanimity? There is equanimity toward internal things, and there is equanimity toward external things. Whichever equanimity toward internal things there is, that factor of equanimity leads to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna. Herein, what is the factor of energy? Whatever mental initiation of energy... right effort, the factor of energy, a path factor, included in the path: this is called "the factor of energy".

Whatever tranquillity, tranquillisation, calming, thorough calming, and the state of having been thoroughly calmed, of the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness — the factor of tranquillity: this is called "the factor of tranquillity".
Herein, what is the factor of concentration? Whatever steadiness of mind... right concentration, the factor of concentration, a path factor, included in the path: this is called "the factor of concentration".
Herein, what is the factor of equanimity? Whatever equanimity, observing with equanimity, watching with equanimity, and neutrality of mind — the factor of equanimity: this is called "the factor of equanimity". ##### Triads ^2-10-3-1-0

484. May be wholesome, may be neutral. The factor of joy is joined with pleasant feeling; the six factors may be joined with pleasant feeling, or may be joined with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. May be things that produce a result, may be things having the nature to produce a result. They are not clung to and not able to be clung to. They are not defiled and not open to defilement. May have applied and sustained thought, may have only sustained thought, or may have neither. The factor of joy is not accompanied by joy — it is accompanied by happiness, not accompanied by equanimity; the six factors may be accompanied by joy, may be accompanied by happiness, or may be accompanied by equanimity. They are to be abandoned by neither seeing nor development. They are rooted in neither what is to be abandoned by seeing nor what is to be abandoned by development. May lead to dismantling, may neither lead to accumulation nor to dismantling. May be still in training, may be beyond training. They are measureless. They have a measureless object. They are superior. May be fixed in rightness, may be unfixed. They do not have the path as object; may have the path as root, may have the path as dominant factor; it should not be said without qualification that they have the path as root, or that they have the path as dominant factor. May be arisen, may be unarisen, may be bound to arise. May be past, may be future, may be present. It should not be said that they have a past object, a future object, or a present object. May be internal, may be external, may be both internal and external. They have an external object. They are invisible and without resistance. ^2-484

##### Pairs ^2-10-3-2-0

485. The factor of investigation is a root; the six factors are joined with a root. The factor of investigation is both a root and rooted; the six factors should not be said to be both a root and rooted — they are rooted but not themselves a root. The factor of investigation is both a root and joined with a root; the six factors should not be said to be both a root and joined with a root — they are joined with a root but not themselves a root. The six factors are not a root, but are rooted; the factor of investigation should not be said to be either "not a root, but rooted" or "not a root and rootless". They have conditions. They are conditioned. They are invisible. They offer no resistance. They are immaterial. They are beyond the world. They are knowable by some kinds of consciousness, not knowable by others. They are not themselves a mental taint. They are free of mental taints. They are dissociated from a mental taint. They should not be said to be both a mental taint and subject to mental taints, or to be subject to mental taints but not itself a mental taint. They should not be said to be both a mental taint and joined with a mental taint, or to be joined with a mental taint but not itself a mental taint. They are dissociated from a mental taint and free of it. They are not themselves a fetter... not themselves a tie... not themselves a flood... not themselves a yoke... not themselves a hindrance... not themselves wrong grasping... They have an object. They are not mind. They are mental factors. They are joined with mind. They are mingled with mind. They originate from mind. They co-arise with mind. They follow mind. They are mingled with mind and originating from mind. They are mingled with mind, originating from mind, and co-arising with mind. They are mingled with mind, originating from mind, and following mind. They are external. They are not derived. They are not clung to. They are not themselves clinging... not themselves a defilement... They are not to be abandoned by seeing. They are not to be abandoned by development. They are not rooted in what is to be abandoned by seeing. They are not rooted in what is to be abandoned by development. They may have applied thought, or may lack applied thought. They may have sustained thought, or may lack sustained thought.
The factor of joy lacks joy; the six factors may have joy, or may lack joy. The factor of joy is not accompanied by joy; the six factors may be accompanied by joy, or may not be accompanied by joy. The factor of joy is accompanied by happiness; the six factors may be accompanied by happiness, or may not be accompanied by happiness. The factor of joy is not accompanied by equanimity; the six factors may be accompanied by equanimity, or may not be accompanied by equanimity. They do not belong to the sense sphere. They do not belong to the fine-material sphere. They do not belong to the immaterial sphere. They are unincluded. They may lead to liberation, or may not lead to liberation. They may be fixed, or may be unfixed. They are unsurpassed. They are peaceful.

### Analysis of the Path Factors ^2-11-0

#### Discourse Classification ^2-11-1-0

486. The noble eightfold path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. ^2-486

487. Herein, what is right view? Knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of suffering — this is called "right view".
Herein, what is right intention? The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill-will, the intention of harmlessness — this is called "right intention".
Herein, what is right speech? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter — this is called "right speech".
Herein, what is right action? Abstaining from killing living beings, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct — this is called "right action".
Herein, what is right livelihood? Here a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, makes his living by right livelihood — this is called "right livelihood".
Herein, what is right effort? Here a monk, for the non-arising of unarisen bad, unwholesome states, generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives; for the abandoning of arisen bad, unwholesome states, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives; for the arising of unarisen wholesome states, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives; for the continuation, non-confusion, increase, expansion, and fulfilment by development of arisen wholesome states, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives — this is called "right effort".
Herein, what is right mindfulness? Here a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; dwells contemplating mental objects in mental objects, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world — this is called "right mindfulness".
Herein, what is right concentration? Here a monk, quite secluded from sense pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first absorption, accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion. With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second absorption, which has internal confidence and concentration of mind, is without applied thought and without sustained thought, and has joy and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of joy, he dwells with equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third absorption, of which the noble ones say: "one of equanimity and mindfulness dwells happily". With the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of pain, and with the earlier disappearance of gladness and sadness, he enters and dwells in the fourth absorption, which is neither painful nor pleasant, and which has purity of mindfulness through equanimity — this is called "right concentration". ^2-487

488. The noble eightfold path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. ^2-488

489. Herein, what is right view? Here a monk develops right view that inclines toward seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and ripens in release; he develops right intention... he develops right speech... he develops right action... he develops right livelihood... he develops right effort... he develops right mindfulness... he develops right concentration that inclines toward seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and ripens in release.
