##### The Exposition of the Ones ^2-16-11-1-0

761. The five consciousnesses are only not a root, only rootless, only dissociated from roots, only with conditions, only conditioned, only immaterial, only worldly, only subject to mental taints, only bound by fetters, only bound by ties, only swept by floods, only bound by yokes, only hindered by hindrances, only wrongly grasped, only subject to clinging, only open to defilement, only neutral, only having an object, only not mental factors, only resultant, only clung-to and subject to clinging, only undefiled yet open to defilement, only not accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, only not without applied thought while having only sustained thought, only without applied thought and without sustained thought, only not accompanied by joy, only not to be abandoned by seeing or by development, only lacking a root to be abandoned by seeing or by development, only leading neither to accumulation nor to dismantling, only neither in training nor beyond training, only limited, only sense-sphere, only not fine-material-sphere, only not immaterial-sphere, only included, only not unincluded, only not fixed, only not emancipating, once arisen, cognizable only by mind-consciousness, only impermanent, only overcome by aging. ^2-761

762. The five consciousnesses have an arisen basis and an arisen object: they arise when the basis has arisen and the object has arisen.
Have a basis that arose earlier and an object that arose earlier: they arise when the basis arose earlier and the object arose earlier.
Have an internal basis and an external object: for the five consciousnesses, the basis is internal and the object is external.
Have an unmixed basis and an unmixed object: they arise when the basis is unmixed and the object is unmixed.
Have different bases and different objects: the basis and object of eye-consciousness are one thing, the basis and object of ear-consciousness are another, the basis and object of nose-consciousness are another, the basis and object of tongue-consciousness are another, the basis and object of body-consciousness are another. ^2-762

763. Do not experience one another's field and range: ear-consciousness does not experience the field and range of eye-consciousness, and eye-consciousness does not experience the field and range of ear-consciousness. Nose-consciousness does not experience the field and range of eye-consciousness, and eye-consciousness does not experience the field and range of nose-consciousness. Tongue-consciousness does not experience the field and range of eye-consciousness, and eye-consciousness does not experience the field and range of tongue-consciousness. Body-consciousness does not experience the field and range of eye-consciousness, and eye-consciousness does not experience the field and range of body-consciousness. ... eye-consciousness does not experience the field and range of ear-consciousness... of nose-consciousness... of tongue-consciousness... of body-consciousness, and body-consciousness does not experience the field and range of eye-consciousness. Ear-consciousness does not experience the field and range of body-consciousness, and body-consciousness does not experience the field and range of ear-consciousness. Nose-consciousness does not experience the field and range of body-consciousness, and body-consciousness does not experience the field and range of nose-consciousness. Tongue-consciousness does not experience the field and range of body-consciousness, and body-consciousness does not experience the field and range of tongue-consciousness. ^2-763

764. Do not arise without adverting: they arise for one who is adverting.
Do not arise without attention: they arise for one who is attending.
Do not arise in a fixed order: they do not arise in a [fixed] sequence.
Do not arise simultaneously: they do not arise in the same moment. ^2-764

765. Do not arise immediately after one another: immediately after eye-consciousness has arisen, ear-consciousness does not arise, and immediately after ear-consciousness has arisen, eye-consciousness does not arise. Immediately after eye-consciousness has arisen, nose-consciousness does not arise, and immediately after nose-consciousness has arisen, eye-consciousness does not arise. Immediately after eye-consciousness has arisen, tongue-consciousness does not arise, and immediately after tongue-consciousness has arisen, eye-consciousness does not arise. Immediately after eye-consciousness has arisen, body-consciousness does not arise, and immediately after body-consciousness has arisen, eye-consciousness does not arise. ... immediately after ear-consciousness... nose-consciousness... tongue-consciousness... body-consciousness has arisen, eye-consciousness does not arise, and immediately after eye-consciousness has arisen, body-consciousness does not arise. Immediately after body-consciousness has arisen, ear-consciousness does not arise, and immediately after ear-consciousness has arisen, body-consciousness does not arise. Immediately after body-consciousness has arisen, nose-consciousness does not arise, and immediately after nose-consciousness has arisen, body-consciousness does not arise. Immediately after body-consciousness has arisen, tongue-consciousness does not arise, and immediately after tongue-consciousness has arisen, body-consciousness does not arise. ^2-765

766. The five consciousnesses are without active engagement: for the five consciousnesses there is no turning, no engagement, no adverting, and no attention.
By means of the five consciousnesses one does not discern anything at all: by means of the five consciousnesses one does not discern anything at all.
Apart from mere impingement: apart from mere impact.
Even immediately after the five consciousnesses, one does not discern anything at all: even immediately after the five consciousnesses, the mind element also does not discern anything at all.
By means of the five consciousnesses one does not set up any posture: by means of the five consciousnesses one does not set up any posture – walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
Even immediately after the five consciousnesses, one does not set up any posture: even immediately after the five consciousnesses, the mind element also does not set up any posture – walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
By means of the five consciousnesses one does not initiate bodily action or verbal action: by means of the five consciousnesses one does not initiate bodily action or verbal action.
Even immediately after the five consciousnesses, one does not initiate bodily action or verbal action: even immediately after the five consciousnesses, the mind element also does not initiate bodily action or verbal action.
By means of the five consciousnesses one does not undertake a wholesome or unwholesome state: by means of the five consciousnesses one does not undertake a wholesome or unwholesome state.
Even immediately after the five consciousnesses, one does not undertake a wholesome or unwholesome state: even immediately after the five consciousnesses, the mind element also does not undertake a wholesome or unwholesome state.
By means of the five consciousnesses one does not enter into an attainment or emerge from it: by means of the five consciousnesses one does not enter into an attainment or emerge from it.
Even immediately after the five consciousnesses, one does not enter into an attainment or emerge from it: even immediately after the five consciousnesses, the mind element also does not enter into an attainment or emerge from it.
By means of the five consciousnesses one does not pass away or arise: by means of the five consciousnesses one does not pass away or arise.
Even immediately after the five consciousnesses, one does not pass away or arise: even immediately after the five consciousnesses, the mind element also does not pass away or arise.
By means of the five consciousnesses one does not sleep, wake up, or dream: by means of the five consciousnesses one does not sleep, wake up, or dream.
Even immediately after the five consciousnesses, one does not sleep, wake up, or dream: even immediately after the five consciousnesses, the mind element also does not sleep, wake up, or dream. Thus wisdom is what makes clear the true nature of things.
Thus, by way of one kind, is the basis of knowledge.
The Ones. ^2-766

##### The Exposition of the Twos ^2-16-11-2-0

767. (1) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is worldly wisdom; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is world-transcending wisdom.
(2) All wisdom whatsoever can be known by another in some way, and cannot be known by another in some way.
(3) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom subject to mental taints; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom free of mental taints.
(4) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom dissociated from mental taints yet subject to them; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom dissociated from mental taints and free of them.
(5) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom bound by fetters; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom not bound by fetters.
(6) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom dissociated from fetters yet bound by them; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom dissociated from fetters and not bound by them.
(7) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom bound by ties; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom not bound by ties.
(8) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom dissociated from ties yet bound by them; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom dissociated from ties and not bound by them.
(9) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom swept by floods; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom not swept by floods.
(10) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom dissociated from floods yet swept by them; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom dissociated from floods and not swept by them.
(11) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom bound by yokes; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom not bound by yokes.
(12) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom dissociated from yokes yet bound by them; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom dissociated from yokes and not bound by them.
(13) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom hindered by hindrances; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom not hindered by hindrances.
(14) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom dissociated from hindrances yet hindered by them; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom dissociated from hindrances and not hindered by them.
(15) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wrongly grasped wisdom; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom not wrongly grasped.
(16) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom dissociated from wrong grasping yet wrongly grasped; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom dissociated from wrong grasping and not wrongly grasped.
(17) Wisdom in the resultant states in the three planes is clung-to wisdom; wisdom in the wholesome states in the three planes, in the functional-neutral states in the three planes, and in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom not clung to.
(18) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom subject to clinging; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom not subject to clinging.
(19) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom dissociated from clinging yet subject to it; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom dissociated from clinging and not subject to it.
(20) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom open to defilement; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom not open to defilement.
(21) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is wisdom dissociated from defilements yet open to defilement; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom dissociated from defilements and not open to defilement.
(22) Wisdom joined with applied thought is wisdom accompanied by applied thought; wisdom dissociated from applied thought is wisdom without applied thought.
(23) Wisdom joined with sustained thought is wisdom accompanied by sustained thought; wisdom dissociated from sustained thought is wisdom without sustained thought.
(24) Wisdom joined with joy is wisdom with joy; wisdom dissociated from joy is wisdom without joy.
(25) Wisdom joined with joy is wisdom accompanied by joy; wisdom dissociated from joy is wisdom not accompanied by joy.
(26) Wisdom joined with happiness is wisdom accompanied by happiness; wisdom dissociated from happiness is wisdom not accompanied by happiness.
(27) Wisdom joined with equanimity is wisdom accompanied by equanimity; wisdom dissociated from equanimity is wisdom not accompanied by equanimity.
(28) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states of the sense-sphere is sense-sphere wisdom; fine-material-sphere wisdom, immaterial-sphere wisdom, and wisdom not included are wisdom that is not sense-sphere.
(29) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states of the fine-material sphere is fine-material-sphere wisdom; sense-sphere wisdom, immaterial-sphere wisdom, and wisdom not included are wisdom that is not fine-material-sphere.
(30) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states of the immaterial sphere is immaterial-sphere wisdom; sense-sphere wisdom, fine-material-sphere wisdom, and wisdom not included are wisdom that is not immaterial-sphere.
(31) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is included wisdom; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom not included.
(32) Wisdom in the four paths is emancipating wisdom; wisdom in the wholesome states in the three planes, the resultant states in the four planes, and the functional-neutral states in the three planes is wisdom that is not emancipating.
(33) Wisdom in the four paths is fixed wisdom; wisdom in the wholesome states in the three planes, the resultant states in the four planes, and the functional-neutral states in the three planes is wisdom that is not fixed.
(34) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states in the three planes is surpassable wisdom; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is unsurpassed wisdom.
(35) Herein, what is wisdom that produces the goal?
Wisdom in the functional-neutral states in the four planes, belonging to an arahant who is producing direct knowledge or producing an attainment, is wisdom that produces the goal; wisdom in the resultant states in the four planes, belonging to an arahant, that arises together with an arisen direct knowledge or an arisen attainment, is wisdom whose goal has been produced.
Thus, by way of two kinds, is the basis of knowledge.
The Twos. ^2-767

##### The Exposition of the Threes ^2-16-11-3-0

768. (1. a) Herein, what is wisdom born of thought?
With regard to occupations arranged through effort, or crafts arranged through effort, or fields of expertise arranged through effort, or the ownership of deeds, or conformity with the truths, or the thought "material form is impermanent" or "feeling... perception... formations... consciousness is impermanent" – whatever conforming acceptance, view, liking, approval, and reflective acceptance of such a kind one gains without having heard it from another – this is called "wisdom born of thought".
(b) Herein, what is wisdom born of hearing? With regard to occupations arranged through effort, or crafts arranged through effort, or fields of expertise arranged through effort, or the ownership of deeds, or conformity with the truths, or the thought "material form is impermanent" or "feeling... perception... formations... consciousness is impermanent" – whatever conforming acceptance, view, liking, approval, and reflective acceptance of such a kind one gains through having heard it from another – this is called "wisdom born of hearing".
(c) All wisdom whatsoever of one who has attained is wisdom born of development. ^2-768

769. (2. a) Herein, what is wisdom born of giving? Whatever wisdom arises when undertaking and accomplishing giving – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "wisdom born of giving".
(b) Herein, what is wisdom born of virtue? Whatever wisdom arises when undertaking and accomplishing virtue – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "wisdom born of virtue".
(c) All wisdom whatsoever of one who has attained is wisdom born of development. ^2-769

770. (3. a) Herein, what is wisdom in the higher virtue? Whatever wisdom arises in one who is restraining himself with the restraint of the code of conduct – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "wisdom in the higher virtue".
(b) Herein, what is wisdom in the higher mind? Whatever wisdom arises in one who is attaining the fine-material or immaterial attainment – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "wisdom in the higher mind".
(c) Herein, what is wisdom in the higher wisdom? Wisdom in the four paths and four fruits – this is called "wisdom in the higher wisdom". ^2-770

771. (4. a) Herein, what is skill in gain? "For one attending to these states, unarisen unwholesome states do not arise, and arisen unwholesome states are abandoned. Or, for one attending to these states, unarisen wholesome states arise, and arisen wholesome states lead to growth, abundance, development, and fulfilment" – whatever wisdom there is on that occasion – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "skill in gain".
(b) Herein, what is skill in loss? "For one attending to these states, unarisen wholesome states do not arise, and arisen wholesome states cease. Or, for one attending to these states, unarisen unwholesome states arise, and arisen unwholesome states lead to growth and abundance" – whatever wisdom there is on that occasion – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "skill in loss".
(c) All wisdom that is a means to that end is skill in means. ^2-771

772. (5. a) Wisdom in the resultant states in the four planes is resultant wisdom.
(b) Wisdom in the wholesome states in the four planes is wisdom productive of a result.
(c) Wisdom in the functional-neutral states in the three planes is wisdom that is neither resultant nor productive of a result. ^2-772

773. (6. a) Wisdom in the resultant states in the three planes is wisdom clung-to and subject to clinging.
(b) Wisdom in the wholesome states in the three planes and the functional-neutral states in the three planes is wisdom not clung-to but subject to clinging.
(c) Wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom not clung-to and not subject to clinging. ^2-773

774. (7. a) Wisdom joined with applied thought and sustained thought is wisdom accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought.
(b) Wisdom dissociated from applied thought but joined with sustained thought is wisdom without applied thought but with only sustained thought.
(c) Wisdom dissociated from applied thought and sustained thought is wisdom without applied thought and without sustained thought. ^2-774

775. (8. a) Wisdom joined with joy is wisdom accompanied by joy.
(b) Wisdom joined with happiness is wisdom accompanied by happiness.
(c) Wisdom joined with equanimity is wisdom accompanied by equanimity. ^2-775

776. (9. a) Wisdom in the wholesome states in the three planes is wisdom leading to accumulation.
(b) Wisdom in the four paths is wisdom leading to dismantling.
(c) Wisdom in the resultant states in the four planes and the functional-neutral states in the three planes is wisdom leading neither to accumulation nor to dismantling. ^2-776

777. (10. a) Wisdom in the four paths and the three lower fruits is wisdom of one in training.
(b) Wisdom in the highest fruit, arahantship, is wisdom of one beyond training.
(c) Wisdom in the wholesome states in the three planes, the resultant states in the three planes, and the functional-neutral states in the three planes is wisdom pertaining neither to one in training nor to one beyond training. ^2-777

778. (11. a) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states of the sense-sphere is limited wisdom.
(b) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres is exalted wisdom.
(c) Wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is measureless wisdom. ^2-778

779. (12. a) Herein, what is wisdom having a limited object? Whatever wisdom arises with regard to a limited state – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "wisdom having a limited object". ^2-779

780. (b) Herein, what is wisdom having an exalted object? Whatever wisdom arises with regard to an exalted state – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "wisdom having an exalted object". ^2-780

781. (c) Herein, what is wisdom having a measureless object? Whatever wisdom arises with regard to a measureless state – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "wisdom having a measureless object". ^2-781

782. (13. a) Herein, what is wisdom having the path as object? Whatever wisdom arises with regard to the noble path – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "wisdom having the path as object".
(b) Wisdom in the four paths is wisdom having the path as root. ^2-782

783. (c) Herein, what is wisdom having the path as predominant factor? Whatever wisdom arises having made the noble path a predominant factor – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "wisdom having the path as predominant factor". ^2-783

784. (14) Wisdom in the resultant states in the four planes may be arisen, may be due to arise, but should not be said to be not-yet-arisen. Wisdom in the wholesome states in the four planes and the functional-neutral states in the three planes may be arisen, may be not-yet-arisen, but should not be said to be due to arise. ^2-784

785. (15) All wisdom whatsoever may be past, may be future, may be present. ^2-785

786. (16. a) Herein, what is wisdom having a past object? Whatever wisdom arises with regard to a past state – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "wisdom having a past object". ^2-786

787. (b) Herein, what is wisdom having a future object? Whatever wisdom arises with regard to a future state – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "wisdom having a future object". ^2-787

788. (c) Herein, what is wisdom having a present object? Whatever wisdom arises with regard to a present state – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "wisdom having a present object". ^2-788

789. (17) All wisdom whatsoever may be internal, may be external, may be internal-and-external. ^2-789

790. (18. a) Herein, what is wisdom having an internal object? Whatever wisdom arises with regard to an internal state – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "wisdom having an internal object". ^2-790

791. (b) Herein, what is wisdom having an external object? Whatever wisdom arises with regard to an external state – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "wisdom having an external object". ^2-791

792. (c) Herein, what is wisdom having an internal-and-external object? Whatever wisdom arises with regard to an internal-and-external state – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "wisdom having an internal-and-external object".
Thus, by way of three kinds, is the basis of knowledge.
The Threes. ^2-792

##### The Exposition of the Fours ^2-16-11-4-0

793. (1. a) Herein, what is knowledge of the ownership of deeds? "There is what is given, there is what is offered, there is what is sacrificed; there is fruit and result of deeds well done and badly done; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are beings spontaneously reborn; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who have travelled and practised rightly, who having realised this world and the other world by direct knowledge for themselves make it known" – whatever wisdom there is of such a kind – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "knowledge of the ownership of deeds". Except for knowledge conforming to the truths, all wholesome wisdom that is subject to mental taints is knowledge of the ownership of deeds.
(b) Herein, what is knowledge conforming to the truths? Whatever conforming acceptance, view, liking, approval, and reflective acceptance of the kind "material form is impermanent" or "feeling... perception... formations... consciousness is impermanent" – this is called "knowledge conforming to the truths".
(c) Wisdom in the four paths is knowledge of one who possesses the path.
(d) Wisdom in the four fruits is knowledge of one who possesses the fruit. ^2-793

794. (2) Knowledge of one who possesses the path is knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
(a) Herein, what is knowledge of suffering? Whatever wisdom arises with regard to suffering – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "knowledge of suffering".
(b-d) With regard to the origin of suffering... with regard to the cessation of suffering... with regard to the practice leading to the cessation of suffering, whatever wisdom arises – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering". ^2-794

795. (3) Wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states of the sense-sphere is sense-sphere wisdom; wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states of the fine-material sphere is fine-material-sphere wisdom; wisdom in the wholesome and neutral states of the immaterial sphere is immaterial-sphere wisdom; wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is wisdom that is not included. ^2-795

796. (4. a) Herein, what is knowledge of principles? Wisdom in the four paths and four fruits is knowledge of principles.
(b) By means of this principle known, seen, attained, understood, and fathomed, one applies a method to the past and the future: "Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past directly knew suffering, directly knew the origin of suffering, directly knew the cessation of suffering, directly knew the practice leading to the cessation of suffering – all of them directly knew this same suffering, this same origin of suffering, this same cessation of suffering, this same practice leading to the cessation of suffering. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will directly know suffering, will directly know the origin of suffering, will directly know the cessation of suffering, will directly know the practice leading to the cessation of suffering – all of them will directly know this same suffering, this same origin of suffering, this same cessation of suffering, this same practice leading to the cessation of suffering" – whatever wisdom there is on that occasion – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "inferential knowledge".
(c) Herein, what is knowledge of encompassing? Herein a monk understands, having encompassed with his own mind the mind of other beings and other persons. He understands a mind with lust as "a mind with lust", a mind without lust as "a mind without lust"; a mind with hatred as "a mind with hatred", a mind without hatred as "a mind without hatred"; a mind with delusion as "a mind with delusion", a mind without delusion as "a mind without delusion"; a contracted mind as "a contracted mind", a distracted mind as "a distracted mind"; an exalted mind as "an exalted mind", an unexalted mind as "an unexalted mind"; a surpassable mind as "a surpassable mind", an unsurpassable mind as "an unsurpassable mind"; a concentrated mind as "a concentrated mind", an unconcentrated mind as "an unconcentrated mind"; a liberated mind as "a liberated mind", an unliberated mind as "an unliberated mind" – whatever wisdom there is on that occasion – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "knowledge of encompassing".
(d) Except for knowledge of principles, inferential knowledge, and knowledge of encompassing, the remaining wisdom is conventional knowledge. ^2-796

797. (5. a) Herein, what is wisdom for accumulation and not for dismantling? Wisdom in sense-sphere wholesome states is wisdom for accumulation and not for dismantling.
(b) Wisdom in the four paths is wisdom for dismantling and not for accumulation.
(c) Wisdom in the fine-material-sphere and immaterial-sphere wholesome states is wisdom for both accumulation and dismantling.
(d) The remaining wisdom is neither for accumulation nor for dismantling. ^2-797

798. (6. a) Herein, what is wisdom for disenchantment and not for penetration? The wisdom by which one becomes free of lust for sensual pleasures, but does not penetrate the higher knowledges or the truths – this is called "wisdom for disenchantment and not for penetration".
(b) That same wisdom, while becoming free of lust for sensual pleasures, penetrating the higher knowledges but not the truths – this is called "wisdom for penetration and not for disenchantment".
(c) Wisdom in the four paths is wisdom for both disenchantment and penetration.
(d) The remaining wisdom is neither for disenchantment nor for penetration. ^2-798

799. (7. a) Herein, what is wisdom that shares in decline? For one who has gained the first jhāna, perception and attention connected with sensual pleasures occur – this is wisdom that shares in decline.
(b) Mindfulness that is consistent with that state stands firm – this is wisdom that shares in stability.
(c) Perception and attention connected with the absence of applied thought occur – this is wisdom that shares in distinction.
(d) Perception and attention connected with disenchantment, bound up with dispassion, occur – this is wisdom that shares in breaking through. For one who has gained the second jhāna, perception and attention connected with applied thought occur – this is wisdom that shares in decline. Mindfulness that is consistent with that state stands firm – this is wisdom that shares in stability. Perception and attention connected with equanimity occur – this is wisdom that shares in distinction. Perception and attention connected with disenchantment, bound up with dispassion, occur – this is wisdom that shares in breaking through. For one who has gained the third jhāna, perception and attention connected with joy and happiness occur – this is wisdom that shares in decline. Mindfulness that is consistent with that state stands firm – this is wisdom that shares in stability. Perception and attention connected with neither-pain-nor-pleasure occur – this is wisdom that shares in distinction. Perception and attention connected with disenchantment, bound up with dispassion, occur – this is wisdom that shares in breaking through. For one who has gained the fourth jhāna, perception and attention connected with equanimity occur – this is wisdom that shares in decline. Mindfulness that is consistent with that state stands firm – this is wisdom that shares in stability. Perception and attention connected with the base of boundless space occur – this is wisdom that shares in distinction. Perception and attention connected with disenchantment, bound up with dispassion, occur – this is wisdom that shares in breaking through. For one who has gained the base of boundless space, perception and attention connected with material form occur – this is wisdom that shares in decline. Mindfulness that is consistent with that state stands firm – this is wisdom that shares in stability. Perception and attention connected with the base of boundless consciousness occur – this is wisdom that shares in distinction. Perception and attention connected with disenchantment, bound up with dispassion, occur – this is wisdom that shares in breaking through. For one who has gained the base of boundless consciousness, perception and attention connected with the base of boundless space occur – this is wisdom that shares in decline. Mindfulness that is consistent with that state stands firm – this is wisdom that shares in stability. Perception and attention connected with the base of nothingness occur – this is wisdom that shares in distinction. Perception and attention connected with disenchantment, bound up with dispassion, occur – this is wisdom that shares in breaking through. For one who has gained the base of nothingness, perception and attention connected with the base of boundless consciousness occur – this is wisdom that shares in decline. Mindfulness that is consistent with that state stands firm – this is wisdom that shares in stability. Perception and attention connected with the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception occur – this is wisdom that shares in distinction. Perception and attention connected with disenchantment, bound up with dispassion, occur – this is wisdom that shares in breaking through. ^2-799

800. (8) Herein, what are the four analytical knowledges? The analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of principles, the analytical knowledge of language, and the analytical knowledge of ready understanding. Knowledge of meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning; knowledge of principles is the analytical knowledge of principles; knowledge of the expression of principles in language on that occasion is the analytical knowledge of language; knowledge of [these] knowledges is the analytical knowledge of ready understanding. These are the four analytical knowledges. ^2-800

801. (9) Herein, what are the four kinds of practice? Painful practice with slow direct knowledge, painful practice with quick direct knowledge, pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge, and pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge.
(a) Herein, what is painful practice with slow direct knowledge? Whatever wisdom arises in one who, with difficulty and hardship, is generating concentration, and directly knows that state slowly – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "painful practice with slow direct knowledge".
(b) Herein, what is painful practice with quick direct knowledge? Whatever wisdom arises in one who, with difficulty and hardship, is generating concentration, and directly knows that state quickly – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "painful practice with quick direct knowledge".
(c) Herein, what is pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge? Whatever wisdom arises in one who, without difficulty or hardship, is generating concentration, and directly knows that state slowly – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge".
(d) Herein, what is pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge? Whatever wisdom arises in one who, without difficulty or hardship, is generating concentration, and directly knows that state quickly – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge". These are the four kinds of practice. ^2-801

802. (10) Herein, what are the four objects? Limited wisdom with a limited object, limited wisdom with a measureless object, measureless wisdom with a limited object, and measureless wisdom with a measureless object.
(a) Herein, what is limited wisdom with a limited object? Whatever wisdom arises in one who has not gained mastery of concentration and is pervading a small object – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "limited wisdom with a limited object".
(b) Herein, what is limited wisdom with a measureless object? Whatever wisdom arises in one who has not gained mastery of concentration and is pervading a vast object – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "limited wisdom with a measureless object".
(c) Herein, what is measureless wisdom with a limited object? Whatever wisdom arises in one who has gained mastery of concentration and is pervading a small object – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "measureless wisdom with a limited object".
(d) Herein, what is measureless wisdom with a measureless object? Whatever wisdom arises in one who has gained mastery of concentration and is pervading a vast object – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "measureless wisdom with a measureless object". These are the four objects.
(11) Knowledge of one who possesses the path is knowledge of aging-and-death, knowledge of the origin of aging-and-death, knowledge of the cessation of aging-and-death, and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of aging-and-death.
(a) Herein, what is knowledge of aging-and-death? Whatever wisdom arises with regard to aging-and-death – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "knowledge of aging-and-death".
(b-d) With regard to the origin of aging-and-death... with regard to the cessation of aging-and-death... with regard to the practice leading to the cessation of aging-and-death, whatever wisdom arises – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of aging-and-death". ^2-802

803. (12-21) Knowledge of one who possesses a principle is knowledge of birth... knowledge of existence... knowledge of clinging... knowledge of craving... knowledge of feeling... knowledge of contact... knowledge of the six sense-fields... knowledge of name-and-form... knowledge of consciousness... knowledge of formations, knowledge of the origin of formations, knowledge of the cessation of formations, and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of formations.
Herein, what is knowledge of formations? Whatever wisdom arises with regard to formations – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "knowledge of formations".
With regard to the origin of formations... with regard to the cessation of formations... with regard to the practice leading to the cessation of formations, whatever wisdom arises – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is called "knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of formations. Thus, by way of four kinds, is the basis of knowledge.
The Fours. ^2-803

##### The Exposition of the Fives ^2-16-11-5-0

804. (1) Herein, what is right concentration with five factors? Pervasion by joy, pervasion by happiness, pervasion of mind, pervasion by light, and the theme of reviewing. Wisdom in the two jhānas is pervasion by joy. Wisdom in the three jhānas is pervasion by happiness. Knowledge of another's mind is pervasion of mind. The divine eye is pervasion by light. The knowledge of reviewing, for one who has emerged from any given concentration, is the theme of reviewing. This is called right concentration with five factors.
(2) Herein, what is right concentration with five knowledges? "This concentration is pleasant now and also ripens in future happiness" – personal knowledge arises thus. "This concentration is noble and free of worldly attachment" – personal knowledge arises thus. "This concentration is not resorted to by inferior persons" – personal knowledge arises thus. "This concentration is peaceful, sublime, gained through tranquillity, attained through unification of mind, and not reached by forceful suppression" – personal knowledge arises thus. "I enter this concentration mindfully and emerge from it mindfully" – personal knowledge arises thus. This is right concentration with five knowledges. Thus, by way of five kinds, is the basis of knowledge.
The Fives. ^2-804

##### The Exposition of the Sixes ^2-16-11-6-0

805. Herein, what is wisdom found in the six kinds of direct knowledge? Knowledge of psychic power, knowledge of the purified ear element, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of the recollection of past lives, knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings, and knowledge of the destruction of the mental taints – this is wisdom found in the six kinds of direct knowledge. Thus, by way of six kinds, is the basis of knowledge.
The Sixes. ^2-805

##### The Exposition of the Sevens ^2-16-11-7-0

806. Herein, what are the seventy-seven bases of knowledge? Knowledge that "dependent on birth, aging-and-death comes to be"; knowledge that "when birth is absent, there is no aging-and-death"; knowledge that "in the past too, dependent on birth, aging-and-death came to be"; knowledge that "when birth was absent, there was no aging-and-death"; knowledge that "in the future too, dependent on birth, aging-and-death will come to be"; knowledge that "when birth is absent, there will be no aging-and-death". And that knowledge of the stability of principles – knowledge that it too has the nature to be destroyed, to vanish, to fade away, and to cease; knowledge that "dependent on existence, birth comes to be"... knowledge that "dependent on clinging, existence comes to be"... knowledge that "dependent on craving, clinging comes to be"... knowledge that "dependent on feeling, craving comes to be"... knowledge that "dependent on contact, feeling comes to be"... knowledge that "dependent on the six sense-fields, contact comes to be"... knowledge that "dependent on name-and-form, the six sense-fields come to be"... knowledge that "dependent on consciousness, name-and-form comes to be"... knowledge that "dependent on formations, consciousness comes to be"... knowledge that "dependent on ignorance, formations come to be"; knowledge that "when ignorance is absent, there are no formations"; knowledge that "in the past too, dependent on ignorance, formations came to be"; knowledge that "when ignorance was absent, there were no formations"; knowledge that "in the future too, dependent on ignorance, formations will come to be"; knowledge that "when ignorance is absent, there will be no formations". And that knowledge of the stability of principles – knowledge that it too has the nature to be destroyed, to vanish, to fade away, and to cease. These are the seventy-seven bases of knowledge. Thus, by way of seven kinds, is the basis of knowledge.
The Sevens. ^2-806

##### The Exposition of the Eights ^2-16-11-8-0

807. Herein, what is wisdom in the four paths and the four fruits? Wisdom in the path of stream-entry, wisdom in the fruit of stream-entry, wisdom in the path of once-returning, wisdom in the fruit of once-returning, wisdom in the path of non-returning, wisdom in the fruit of non-returning, wisdom in the path of arahantship, wisdom in the fruit of arahantship – this is wisdom in the four paths and the four fruits. Thus, by way of eight kinds, is the basis of knowledge.
The Eights. ^2-807

##### The Exposition of the Nines ^2-16-11-9-0

808. Herein, what is wisdom in the nine progressive dwelling-attainments? Wisdom in the attainment of the first jhāna, wisdom in the attainment of the second jhāna, wisdom in the attainment of the third jhāna, wisdom in the attainment of the fourth jhāna, wisdom in the attainment of the base of boundless space, wisdom in the attainment of the base of boundless consciousness, wisdom in the attainment of the base of nothingness, wisdom in the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the knowledge of reviewing for one who has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling – this is wisdom in the nine progressive dwelling-attainments. Thus, by way of nine kinds, is the basis of knowledge.
The Nines. ^2-808

##### The Exposition of the Tens ^2-16-11-10-0

809. (1) Herein, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible? Herein the Tathāgata understands: "It is impossible, there is no occasion, for a person accomplished in view to take any formation as permanent; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible, indeed, for an ordinary person to take some formation as permanent; that is possible." He understands: "It is impossible, there is no occasion, for a person accomplished in view to take any formation as pleasurable; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible, indeed, for an ordinary person to take some formation as pleasurable; that is possible." He understands: "It is impossible, there is no occasion, for a person accomplished in view to take any state as self; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible, indeed, for an ordinary person to take some state as self; that is possible." He understands: "It is impossible, there is no occasion, for a person accomplished in view to deprive his mother of life; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible, indeed, for an ordinary person to deprive his mother of life; that is possible."
"It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to deprive his father of life... to deprive an arahant of life... to wound a Tathāgata with malicious intent... to cause a schism in the Community... to point to another teacher... to be reborn in an eighth existence; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible, indeed, for an ordinary person to be reborn in an eighth existence; that is possible."
He understands: "It is impossible, there is no occasion, for two fully awakened Buddhas to arise in a single world-system, neither before nor after each other; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible, indeed, for one fully awakened Buddha to arise in a single world-system; that is possible." He understands: "It is impossible, there is no occasion, for two wheel-turning kings to arise in a single world-system, neither before nor after each other; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible, indeed, for one wheel-turning king to arise in a single world-system; that is possible."
He understands: "It is impossible, there is no occasion, for a woman to be a fully awakened arahant; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible, indeed, for a man to be a fully awakened arahant; that is possible." He understands: "It is impossible, there is no occasion, for a woman to be a wheel-turning king; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible, indeed, for a man to be a wheel-turning king; that is possible." He understands: "It is impossible, there is no occasion, for a woman to occupy the position of Sakka, of Māra, or of Brahmā; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible, indeed, for a man to occupy the position of Sakka, of Māra, or of Brahmā; that is possible."
He understands: "It is impossible, there is no occasion, for a desirable, wished-for, agreeable result to be produced by bodily misconduct; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible, indeed, for an undesirable, unwished-for, disagreeable result to be produced by bodily misconduct; that is possible." He understands: "It is impossible for an undesirable result to be produced by verbal misconduct... by mental misconduct... for a desirable, wished-for, agreeable result to be produced; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible for an undesirable, unwished-for, disagreeable result to be produced by verbal misconduct... by mental misconduct; that is possible."
He understands: "It is impossible, there is no occasion, for an undesirable, unwished-for, disagreeable result to be produced by bodily good conduct; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible, indeed, for a desirable, wished-for, agreeable result to be produced by bodily good conduct; that is possible." He understands: "It is impossible for an undesirable result to be produced by verbal good conduct... by mental good conduct; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible for a desirable, wished-for, agreeable result to be produced by verbal good conduct... by mental good conduct; that is possible."
He understands: "It is impossible, there is no occasion, for one possessing bodily misconduct, because of it and on account of it, at the breaking up of the body after death, to be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible, indeed, for one possessing bodily misconduct, because of it and on account of it, at the breaking up of the body after death, to be reborn in a state of misery, an unhappy destination, a lower realm, hell; that is possible." He understands: "It is impossible for one possessing verbal misconduct... possessing mental misconduct, because of it and on account of it, at the breaking up of the body after death, to be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible for one possessing verbal misconduct... possessing mental misconduct, because of it and on account of it, at the breaking up of the body after death, to be reborn in a state of misery, an unhappy destination, a lower realm, hell; that is possible."
He understands: "It is impossible, there is no occasion, for one possessing bodily good conduct, because of it and on account of it, at the breaking up of the body after death, to be reborn in a state of misery, an unhappy destination, a lower realm, hell; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible, indeed, for one possessing bodily good conduct, because of it and on account of it, at the breaking up of the body after death, to be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world; that is possible." He understands: "It is impossible for one possessing verbal good conduct... possessing mental good conduct, because of it and on account of it, at the breaking up of the body after death, to be reborn in a state of misery, an unhappy destination, a lower realm, hell; that is not possible." He understands: "It is possible for one possessing verbal good conduct... possessing mental good conduct, because of it and on account of it, at the breaking up of the body after death, to be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world; that is possible." "Whatever states, taking as their root cause and condition certain other states, constitute that particular case; and whatever states, not taking as their root cause and condition certain other states, constitute that particular impossible case" – whatever wisdom there is on that occasion – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible. ^2-809

810. (2) Herein, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, by way of circumstance and by way of cause, of the result of undertakings of action, past, future, and present? Herein the Tathāgata understands: "There are certain bad undertakings of action that, being obstructed by an accomplishment of destination, do not ripen. There are certain bad undertakings of action that, being obstructed by an accomplishment of personal condition, do not ripen. There are certain bad undertakings of action that, being obstructed by an accomplishment of time, do not ripen. There are certain bad undertakings of action that, being obstructed by an accomplishment of effort, do not ripen.
"There are certain bad undertakings of action that ripen owing to a failure of destination. There are certain bad undertakings of action that ripen owing to a failure of personal condition. There are certain bad undertakings of action that ripen owing to a failure of time. There are certain bad undertakings of action that ripen owing to a failure of effort.
"There are certain good undertakings of action that, being obstructed by a failure of destination, do not ripen. There are certain good undertakings of action that, being obstructed by a failure of personal condition, do not ripen. There are certain good undertakings of action that, being obstructed by a failure of time, do not ripen. There are certain good undertakings of action that, being obstructed by a failure of effort, do not ripen.
"There are certain good undertakings of action that ripen owing to an accomplishment of destination. There are certain good undertakings of action that ripen owing to an accomplishment of personal condition. There are certain good undertakings of action that ripen owing to an accomplishment of time. There are certain good undertakings of action that ripen owing to an accomplishment of effort" – whatever wisdom there is on that occasion – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, by way of circumstance and by way of cause, of the result of undertakings of action, past, future, and present. ^2-810

811. (3) Herein, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of the practice that leads to every destination? Herein the Tathāgata understands: "This path, this practice, leads to hell", he understands; "this path, this practice, leads to the animal realm", he understands; "this path, this practice, leads to the realm of ghosts", he understands; "this path, this practice, leads to the human world", he understands; "this path, this practice, leads to the heavenly world", he understands; "this path, this practice, leads to final liberation", he understands – whatever wisdom there is on that occasion – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of the practice that leads to every destination. ^2-811

812. (4) Herein, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of the world with its many and various elements? Herein the Tathāgata understands the diversity of aggregates, understands the diversity of sense-fields, understands the diversity of elements, understands the diversity of the world with its many and various elements – whatever wisdom there is on that occasion – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of the world with its many and various elements. ^2-812

813. (5) Herein, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of the various inclinations of beings? Herein the Tathāgata understands: "There are beings of inferior inclination, there are beings of refined inclination. Beings of inferior inclination resort to, associate with, and attend upon beings of inferior inclination. Beings of refined inclination resort to, associate with, and attend upon beings of refined inclination.
"In the past too, beings of inferior inclination resorted to, associated with, and attended upon beings of inferior inclination; beings of refined inclination resorted to, associated with, and attended upon beings of refined inclination.
"In the future too, beings of inferior inclination will resort to, associate with, and attend upon beings of inferior inclination; beings of refined inclination will resort to, associate with, and attend upon beings of refined inclination" – whatever wisdom there is on that occasion – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of the various inclinations of beings. ^2-813

814. (6) Herein, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of the maturity of the faculties of other beings and other persons? Herein the Tathāgata understands the disposition of beings, understands the underlying tendency, understands the behaviour, understands the inclination; he understands beings of little dust in the eyes and beings of much dust in the eyes, of sharp faculties and of dull faculties, of good character and of bad character, easy to teach and hard to teach, and those capable and incapable [of progress]. ^2-814

815. What, then, is the disposition of beings? "The world is eternal", or "the world is not eternal", or "the world is finite", or "the world is infinite", or "the soul and the body are the same", or "the soul is one thing, the body another", or "the Tathāgata exists after death", or "the Tathāgata does not exist after death", or "the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death", or "the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death" – thus beings rely either on a view of existence or a view of non-existence. But without approaching either of these two extremes, one gains a conforming acceptance in regard to the states that arise dependent on this-conditionality, and knowledge as it really is. This is the disposition of beings. ^2-815

816. And what is the underlying tendency of beings? The underlying tendencies of beings: the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance. Whatever in the world has an agreeable and pleasing nature, there the underlying tendency to lust lies latent in beings. Whatever in the world has a disagreeable and unpleasing nature, there the underlying tendency to aversion lies latent in beings. Thus, in regard to these two states, ignorance has settled in. Along with it are to be seen conceit, views, and doubt, which share the same basis. This is the underlying tendency of beings. ^2-816

817. And what is the behaviour of beings? Meritorious formation, demeritorious formation, imperturbable formation, whether on a limited plane or a vast plane – this is the behaviour of beings. ^2-817

818. And what is the inclination of beings? There are beings of inferior inclination, there are beings of refined inclination. Beings of inferior inclination resort to, associate with, and attend upon beings of inferior inclination. Beings of refined inclination resort to, associate with, and attend upon beings of refined inclination.
In the past too, beings of inferior inclination resorted to, associated with, and attended upon beings of inferior inclination. Beings of refined inclination resorted to, associated with, and attended upon beings of refined inclination.
In the future too, beings of inferior inclination will resort to, associate with, and attend upon beings of inferior inclination. Beings of refined inclination will resort to, associate with, and attend upon beings of refined inclination. This is the inclination of beings. ^2-818

819. Which are those beings of much dust in the eyes? The ten grounds of defilement: greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, doubt, sloth, restlessness, lack of shame, and lack of moral dread. Those beings for whom these ten grounds of defilement have been practised, developed, cultivated, and have become abundant – these are the beings of much dust in the eyes. ^2-819

820. Which are those beings of little dust in the eyes? Those beings for whom these ten grounds of defilement have not been practised, not developed, not cultivated, and have not become abundant – these are the beings of little dust in the eyes. ^2-820

821. Which are those beings of dull faculties? The five faculties: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. Those beings for whom these five faculties have not been practised, not developed, not cultivated, and have not become abundant – these are the beings of dull faculties. ^2-821

822. Which are those beings of sharp faculties? Those beings for whom these five faculties have been practised, developed, cultivated, and have become abundant – these are the beings of sharp faculties. ^2-822

823. Which are those beings of bad character? Those beings who have a bad disposition, a bad underlying tendency, bad behaviour, a bad inclination, much dust in the eyes, and dull faculties – these are the beings of bad character. ^2-823

824. Which are those beings of good character? Those beings who have a good disposition, good behaviour, a good inclination, little dust in the eyes, and sharp faculties – these are the beings of good character. ^2-824

825. Which are those beings hard to teach? Those beings who are of bad character are the very ones hard to teach. Those beings who are of good character are the very ones easy to teach. ^2-825

826. Which are those beings incapable [of progress]? Those beings possessed of an obstruction of action, possessed of an obstruction of defilement, possessed of an obstruction of result, without faith, without desire, of deficient wisdom, incapable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness among wholesome states – these are the beings incapable [of progress]. ^2-826

827. Which are those beings capable [of progress]? Those beings not possessed of an obstruction of action, not possessed of an obstruction of defilement, not possessed of an obstruction of result, possessing faith, possessing desire, possessing wisdom, capable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness among wholesome states – these are the beings capable [of progress]. Whatever wisdom there is on that occasion – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of the maturity of the faculties of other beings and other persons. ^2-827

828. (7) Herein, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of the defilement, purification, and emergence in respect of the jhānas, the liberations, the concentrations, and the attainments? "Meditator". There are four kinds of meditator. There is a certain meditator who, when accomplishment is present, perceives it as failure; there is a certain meditator who, when failure is present, perceives it as accomplishment; there is a certain meditator who, when accomplishment is present, perceives it as accomplishment; there is a certain meditator who, when failure is present, perceives it as failure – these are the four kinds of meditator.
There are also another four kinds of meditator. There is a certain meditator who enters slowly and emerges quickly; there is a certain meditator who enters quickly and emerges slowly; there is a certain meditator who enters slowly and emerges slowly; there is a certain meditator who enters quickly and emerges quickly – these are the four kinds of meditator.
There are also another four kinds of meditator. There is a certain meditator who is skilled in concentration but not skilled in attainment; there is a certain meditator who is skilled in attainment but not skilled in concentration; there is a certain meditator who is skilled both in concentration and in attainment; there is a certain meditator who is skilled neither in concentration nor in attainment – these are the four kinds of meditator.
"Jhāna". There are four jhānas: the first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna.
"Liberation". There are eight liberations. One possessing material form sees material forms – this is the first liberation.
Not perceiving material form internally, one sees material forms externally – this is the second liberation.
One is resolved only upon the beautiful – this is the third liberation.
With the complete surmounting of perceptions of material form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that "space is boundless", one enters and dwells in the base of boundless space – this is the fourth liberation.
With the complete surmounting of the base of boundless space, aware that "consciousness is boundless", one enters and dwells in the base of boundless consciousness – this is the fifth liberation.
With the complete surmounting of the base of boundless consciousness, aware that "there is nothing", one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness – this is the sixth liberation.
With the complete surmounting of the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception – this is the seventh liberation.
With the complete surmounting of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling – this is the eighth liberation.
"Concentration". There are three concentrations: concentration accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, concentration without applied thought but with only sustained thought, and concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought.
"Attainment". There are nine progressive dwelling-attainments: the attainment of the first jhāna, the attainment of the second jhāna, the attainment of the third jhāna, the attainment of the fourth jhāna, the attainment of the base of boundless space, the attainment of the base of boundless consciousness, the attainment of the base of nothingness, the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
"Defilement" means a state that shares in decline. "Purification" means a state that shares in distinction. "Emergence" – both purification and emergence are emergence, and the emergence from any given concentration is also emergence. Whatever wisdom there is on that occasion – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of the defilement, purification, and emergence in respect of the jhānas, the liberations, the concentrations, and the attainments. ^2-828

829. (8) Herein, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of the recollection of past lives? Herein the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many cycles of contraction, many cycles of expansion, many cycles of contraction and expansion: "There I was named thus, of such a clan, such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life's end; passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere; there too I was named thus, of such a clan, such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life's end; passing away from there, I was reborn here" – thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their modes and details. Whatever wisdom there is on that occasion – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of the recollection of past lives. ^2-829

830. (9) Herein, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of the passing away and rebirth of beings? Herein the Tathāgata, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understands beings as faring according to their deeds: "These beings, indeed, who possessed bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct, who reviled the noble ones, who held wrong view, who undertook deeds based on wrong view – at the breaking up of the body after death, they have been reborn in a state of misery, an unhappy destination, a lower realm, in hell. But these beings, who possessed bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, and mental good conduct, who did not revile the noble ones, who held right view, who undertook deeds based on right view – at the breaking up of the body after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world." Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understands beings as faring according to their deeds. Whatever wisdom there is on that occasion – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of the passing away and rebirth of beings. ^2-830

831. (10) Herein, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of the destruction of the mental taints? Herein the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the mental taints, having realised for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, enters and dwells in it. Whatever wisdom there is on that occasion – understanding... non-delusion, investigation of principles, right view – this is the Tathāgata's knowledge, as it really is, of the destruction of the mental taints.
The Tens.
The Analysis of Knowledge is finished. ^2-831

842. There are eighteen wanderings of craving with respect to what is internal, and eighteen wanderings of craving with respect to what is external; gathering these together and combining them, there are thirty-six wanderings of craving.
