With regard to disagreeable sights, mental displeasure and mental pain tied to household life, unpleasant and painful feeling born of mental contact tied to household life; with regard to disagreeable sounds... disagreeable odors... disagreeable tastes... disagreeable touches... with regard to disagreeable mental objects, mental displeasure and mental pain tied to household life, unpleasant and painful feeling born of mental contact tied to household life — these are the six kinds of grief tied to household life.

##### (13) The six kinds of equanimity tied to household life ^2-17-7-13-0

Herein, what are the six kinds of equanimity tied to household life? With regard to sights that are a basis for equanimity, mental neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant feeling tied to household life, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of mental contact tied to household life; with regard to sounds... odors... tastes... touches that are a basis for equanimity... with regard to mental objects that are a basis for equanimity, mental neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant feeling tied to household life, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of mental contact tied to household life — these are the six kinds of equanimity tied to household life.

##### (14) The six views ^2-17-7-14-0

948. Herein, what are the six views? "I have a self" — such a view arises for him as if true and certain; "I have no self" — such a view arises for him as if true and certain; "I perceive self by means of self" — such a view arises for him as if true and certain; "I perceive not-self by means of self" — such a view arises for him as if true and certain; "I perceive self by means of not-self" — such a view arises for him as if true and certain; or he holds this view: "this self of mine, which speaks and feels, experiences here and there the result of good and bad deeds; this self of mine is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever" — such a view too arises for him as if true and certain. These are the six views.
The Sixes. ^2-948

#### Explanation of Sevens ^2-17-8-0

##### (1) The seven underlying tendencies ^2-17-8-1-0

949. Herein, what are the seven underlying tendencies? The underlying tendency to sensual passion, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to passion for existence, the underlying tendency to ignorance — these are the seven underlying tendencies. ^2-949

##### (2) The seven fetters ^2-17-8-2-0

Herein, what are the seven fetters? The fetter of sensual passion, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of passion for existence, the fetter of ignorance — these are the seven fetters.

##### (3) The seven obsessions ^2-17-8-3-0

Herein, what are the seven obsessions? The obsession of sensual passion, the obsession of aversion, the obsession of conceit, the obsession of views, the obsession of doubt, the obsession of passion for existence, the obsession of ignorance — these are the seven obsessions.

##### (4) The seven things contrary to the true teaching ^2-17-8-4-0

950. Herein, what are the seven things contrary to the true teaching? One lacks faith, one lacks shame, one lacks fear of wrongdoing, one has heard little, one is lazy, one is forgetful, one lacks wisdom — these are the seven things contrary to the true teaching. ^2-950

##### (5) The seven kinds of misconduct ^2-17-8-5-0

Herein, what are the seven kinds of misconduct? Killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter — these are the seven kinds of misconduct.

##### (6) The seven kinds of conceit ^2-17-8-6-0

Herein, what are the seven kinds of conceit? Conceit, exaggerated conceit, conceit beyond conceit, self-belittling conceit, over-estimating conceit, the conceit "I am," wrong conceit — these are the seven kinds of conceit.

##### (7) The seven views ^2-17-8-7-0

951. (a) Herein, what are the seven views? Here some ascetic or brahmin holds this doctrine and view: "when, sir, this self, made of material form, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, is cut off and destroyed with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, then, sir, this self is rightly and completely cut off." So some proclaim the cutting off, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
(b) Another says to him: "sir, there is indeed such a self as you speak of; I do not say there is not. But this self is not thereby rightly and completely cut off. There is, sir, another self, divine, made of material form, belonging to the sense sphere, feeding on solid food. That you do not know or see; I know and see it. That self, sir, is cut off and destroyed with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death; that, sir, is when this self is rightly and completely cut off." So some proclaim the cutting off, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
(c) Another says to him: "sir, there is indeed such a self as you speak of; I do not say there is not. But this self is not thereby rightly and completely cut off. There is, sir, another self, divine, made of material form, mind-made, complete in all its major and minor parts, not deficient in its faculties. That you do not know or see; I know and see it. That self, sir, is cut off... that, sir, is when this self is rightly and completely cut off." So some proclaim the cutting off, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
(d) Another says to him: "sir, there is indeed such a self as you speak of; I do not say there is not. But this self is not thereby rightly and completely cut off. There is, sir, another self which, with the complete transcending of perceptions of material form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite,' has attained the base of infinite space. That you do not know or see; I know and see it. That self, sir, is cut off... that, sir, is when this self is rightly and completely cut off." So some proclaim the cutting off, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
(e) Another says to him: "sir, there is indeed such a self as you speak of; I do not say there is not. But this self is not thereby rightly and completely cut off. There is, sir, another self which, with the complete transcending of the base of infinite space, aware that 'consciousness is infinite,' has attained the base of infinite consciousness. That you do not know or see; I know and see it. That self, sir, is cut off... that, sir, is when this self is rightly and completely cut off." So some proclaim the cutting off, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
(f) Another says to him: "sir, there is indeed such a self as you speak of; I do not say there is not. But this self is not thereby rightly and completely cut off. There is, sir, another self which, with the complete transcending of the base of infinite consciousness, aware that 'there is nothing,' has attained the base of nothingness. That you do not know or see; I know and see it. That self, sir, is cut off... that, sir, is when this self is rightly and completely cut off." So some proclaim the cutting off, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
(g) Another says to him: "sir, there is indeed such a self as you speak of; I do not say there is not. But this self is not thereby rightly and completely cut off. There is, sir, another self which, with the complete transcending of the base of nothingness, has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. That you do not know or see; I know and see it. That self, sir, is cut off and destroyed with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death; that, sir, is when this self is rightly and completely cut off." So some proclaim the cutting off, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being. These are the seven views.
The Sevens. ^2-951

#### Explanation of Eights ^2-17-9-0

##### (1) The eight grounds of defilement ^2-17-9-1-0

952. Herein, what are the eight grounds of defilement? Greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, doubt, dullness, restlessness — these are the eight grounds of defilement. ^2-952

##### (2) The eight grounds of laziness ^2-17-9-2-0

953. Herein, what are the eight grounds of laziness?
(a) Here a monk has some work to do. It occurs to him: "I will have work to do; while doing this work my body will grow tired. Let me lie down." He lies down; he does not rouse energy for attaining what has not been attained, for reaching what has not been reached, for realizing what has not been realized. This is the first ground of laziness.
(b) Again, a monk has done some work. It occurs to him: "I have done work; while doing this work my body has grown tired. Let me lie down." He lies down; he does not rouse energy for attaining what has not been attained, for reaching what has not been reached, for realizing what has not been realized. This is the second ground of laziness.
(c) Again, a monk has a journey to make. It occurs to him: "I will have a journey to make; while making this journey my body will grow tired. Let me lie down." He lies down; he does not rouse energy... This is the third ground of laziness.
(d) Again, a monk has made a journey. It occurs to him: "I have made a journey; while making this journey my body has grown tired. Let me lie down." He lies down; he does not rouse energy... This is the fourth ground of laziness.
(e) Again, a monk walking for almsfood in a village or town does not get as much coarse or fine food as he needs to fill himself. It occurs to him: "I, walking for almsfood in a village or town, did not get as much coarse or fine food as I need to fill myself; my body is tired and unfit for work. Let me lie down." He lies down; he does not rouse energy... This is the fifth ground of laziness.
(f) Again, a monk walking for almsfood in a village or town gets as much coarse or fine food as he needs to fill himself. It occurs to him: "I, walking for almsfood in a village or town, got as much coarse or fine food as I need to fill myself; my body is tired and unfit for work, as heavy as a bean-mash. Let me lie down." He lies down; he does not rouse energy... This is the sixth ground of laziness.
(g) Again, a slight illness has arisen in a monk. It occurs to him: "this slight illness has arisen in me; there is reason to lie down. Let me lie down." He lies down; he does not rouse energy... This is the seventh ground of laziness.
(h) Again, a monk has recently recovered from an illness, not long risen from sickness. It occurs to him: "I have recently recovered from illness, not long risen from sickness; my body is weak and unfit for work. Let me lie down." He lies down; he does not rouse energy for attaining what has not been attained, for reaching what has not been reached, for realizing what has not been realized. This is the eighth ground of laziness. These are the eight grounds of laziness. ^2-953

##### (3) The mind's reaction with regard to the eight worldly conditions ^2-17-9-3-0

954. Herein, what is the mind's reaction with regard to the eight worldly conditions? Intense passion with regard to gain, hostility with regard to loss; intense passion with regard to fame, hostility with regard to disrepute; intense passion with regard to praise, hostility with regard to blame; intense passion with regard to pleasure, hostility with regard to pain — this is the mind's reaction with regard to these eight worldly conditions. ^2-954

##### (4) The eight unworthy modes of speech ^2-17-9-4-0

955. Herein, what are the eight unworthy modes of speech? Claiming to have seen what was not seen, claiming to have heard what was not heard, claiming to have sensed what was not sensed, claiming to have known what was not known; claiming not to have seen what was seen, claiming not to have heard what was heard, claiming not to have sensed what was sensed, claiming not to have known what was known — these are the eight unworthy modes of speech. ^2-955

##### (5) The eight wrong states ^2-17-9-5-0

956. Herein, what are the eight wrong states? Wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration — these are the eight wrong states. ^2-956

##### (6) The eight faults of a person ^2-17-9-6-0

957. Herein, what are the eight faults of a person? (a) Here monks charge a monk with an offense. When charged by the monks with the offense, that monk evades the charge by pleading forgetfulness, saying, "I do not recall, I do not recall." This is the first fault of a person.
(b) Again, monks charge a monk with an offense. When charged by the monks with the offense, that monk turns on the one who charged him, saying, "what value is there in the word of a fool, an incompetent like you! Do you really think you are someone whose word should be heeded?" This is the second fault of a person.
(c) Again, monks charge a monk with an offense. When charged by the monks with the offense, that monk turns the charge back on the accuser himself, saying, "you too have committed such-and-such an offense; you make amends for it first." This is the third fault of a person.
(d) Again, monks charge a monk with an offense. When charged by the monks with the offense, that monk evades one point with another, diverts the talk to something outside the matter, and displays anger, hatred, and displeasure. This is the fourth fault of a person.
(e) Again, monks charge a monk with an offense. When charged by the monks with the offense, that monk waves his arms about in front of the community. This is the fifth fault of a person.
(f) Again, monks charge a monk with an offense. When charged by the monks with the offense, that monk, without regard for the community and without regard for the accuser, being guilty of the offense, goes off wherever he pleases. This is the sixth fault of a person.
(g) Again, monks charge a monk with an offense. When charged by the monks with the offense, that monk says, "I have not committed an offense, nor have I not committed one," and remains silent, troubling the community. This is the seventh fault of a person.
(h) Again, monks charge a monk with an offense. When charged by the monks with the offense, that monk says, "why are you venerable ones so very concerned with me? I will now renounce the training and return to the lower life." Having renounced the training and returned to the lower life, he says, "now, venerable ones, you may be content." This is the eighth fault of a person. These are the eight faults of a person. ^2-957

##### (7) The eight doctrines of non-perception ^2-17-9-7-0

958. Herein, what are the eight doctrines of non-perception? "The self, possessed of material form, is free of affliction after death" — they declare it to be without perception; "the self, immaterial..." "the self, both possessed of material form and immaterial..." "the self, neither possessed of material form nor immaterial..." "the self, finite, is free of affliction after death" — they declare it to be without perception; "the self, infinite, is free of affliction after death" — they declare it to be without perception; "the self, both finite and infinite, is free of affliction after death" — they declare it to be without perception; "the self, neither finite nor infinite, is free of affliction after death" — they declare it to be without perception. These are the eight doctrines of non-perception. ^2-958

##### (8) The eight doctrines of neither-perception-nor-non-perception ^2-17-9-8-0

959. Herein, what are the eight doctrines of neither-perception-nor-non-perception? "The self, possessed of material form, is free of affliction after death" — they declare it to be neither percipient nor non-percipient; "the self, immaterial, is free of affliction after death" — they declare it to be neither percipient nor non-percipient; "the self, both possessed of material form and immaterial, is free of affliction after death" — they declare it to be neither percipient nor non-percipient; "the self, neither possessed of material form nor immaterial, is free of affliction after death" — they declare it to be neither percipient nor non-percipient; "the self, finite, is free of affliction after death" — they declare it to be neither percipient nor non-percipient; "the self, infinite, is free of affliction after death" — they declare it to be neither percipient nor non-percipient; "the self, both finite and infinite, is free of affliction after death" — they declare it to be neither percipient nor non-percipient; "the self, neither finite nor infinite, is free of affliction after death" — they declare it to be neither percipient nor non-percipient. These are the eight doctrines of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The Eights. ^2-959

#### Explanation of Nines ^2-17-10-0

##### (1) The nine grounds of resentment ^2-17-10-1-0

960. Herein, what are the nine grounds of resentment? "He has done me harm," resentment arises; "he is doing me harm," resentment arises; "he will do me harm," resentment arises; "he has done harm... is doing harm... will do harm to one who is dear and pleasing to me," resentment arises; "he has done good... is doing good... will do good to one who is not dear, not pleasing to me," resentment arises. These are the nine grounds of resentment. ^2-960

##### (2) The nine stains of a person ^2-17-10-2-0

961. Herein, what are the nine stains of a person? Anger, contempt, envy, stinginess, deception, treachery, false speech, evil desire, wrong view — these are the nine stains of a person. ^2-961

##### (3) The nine kinds of conceit ^2-17-10-3-0

962. Herein, what are the nine kinds of conceit? The conceit "I, who am better, am better," the conceit "I, who am better, am equal," the conceit "I, who am better, am inferior," the conceit "I, who am equal, am better," the conceit "I, who am equal, am equal," the conceit "I, who am equal, am inferior," the conceit "I, who am inferior, am better," the conceit "I, who am inferior, am equal," the conceit "I, who am inferior, am inferior" — these are the nine kinds of conceit. ^2-962

##### (4) The nine things rooted in craving ^2-17-10-4-0

963. Herein, what are the nine things rooted in craving? With craving as condition, seeking; with seeking as condition, gain; with gain as condition, decision-making; with decision-making as condition, desire and passion; with desire and passion as condition, attachment; with attachment as condition, possessiveness; with possessiveness as condition, stinginess; with stinginess as condition, guarding; and because of guarding, many evil, unwholesome states come into being — taking up the rod, taking up the weapon, conflict, quarreling, dispute, accusation and counter-accusation, malicious talk, and false speech — these are the nine things rooted in craving. ^2-963

##### (5) The nine kinds of agitation ^2-17-10-5-0

964. Herein, what are the nine kinds of agitation? "I am" is an agitation; "I am this" is an agitation; "I am this one here" is an agitation; "I shall be" is an agitation; "I shall be possessed of material form" is an agitation; "I shall be immaterial" is an agitation; "I shall be percipient" is an agitation; "I shall be non-percipient" is an agitation; "I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient" is an agitation — these are the nine kinds of agitation. ^2-964

##### (6-9) The nine kinds of conceiving, and so on ^2-17-10-6-0

965. Herein, what are the nine kinds of conceiving... the nine kinds of trembling... the nine kinds of proliferation... the nine constructed things? "I am" is a constructed thing; "I am this" is a constructed thing; "I am this one here" is a constructed thing; "I shall be" is a constructed thing; "I shall be possessed of material form" is a constructed thing; "I shall be immaterial" is a constructed thing; "I shall be percipient" is a constructed thing; "I shall be non-percipient" is a constructed thing; "I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient" is a constructed thing — these are the nine constructed things.
The Nines. ^2-965

##### (1) The ten grounds of defilement ^2-17-11-1-0

966. Herein, what are the ten grounds of defilement? Greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, doubt, dullness, restlessness, lack of shame, lack of fear of wrongdoing — these are the ten grounds of defilement. ^2-966

##### (2) The ten grounds of resentment ^2-17-11-2-0

967. Herein, what are the ten grounds of resentment? "He has done me harm," resentment arises; "he is doing me harm," resentment arises; "he will do me harm," resentment arises; "he has done harm... is doing harm... will do harm to one who is dear and pleasing to me," resentment arises; "he has done good... is doing good... will do good to one who is not dear, not pleasing to me," resentment arises; or resentment arises without any such basis — these are the ten grounds of resentment. ^2-967

##### (3) The ten courses of unwholesome action ^2-17-11-3-0

968. Herein, what are the ten courses of unwholesome action? Killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, wrong view — these are the ten courses of unwholesome action. ^2-968

##### (4) The ten fetters ^2-17-11-4-0

969. Herein, what are the ten fetters? The fetter of sensual passion, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of adherence to rules and observances, the fetter of passion for existence, the fetter of envy, the fetter of stinginess, the fetter of ignorance — these are the ten fetters. ^2-969

##### (5) The ten wrong states ^2-17-11-5-0

970. Herein, what are the ten wrong states? Wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong knowledge, wrong liberation — these are the ten wrong states. ^2-970

##### (6) The wrong view with ten grounds ^2-17-11-6-0

971. Herein, what is the wrong view with ten grounds? "There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings spontaneously reborn; there are no ascetics and brahmins in the world who are rightly conducted and rightly practicing, who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge, make them known" — this is the wrong view with ten grounds. ^2-971

##### (7) The extremist view with ten grounds ^2-17-11-7-0

972. Herein, what is the extremist view with ten grounds? "The world is eternal," or "the world is not eternal," or "the world is finite," or "the world is infinite," or "the soul and the body are the same," or "the soul and the body are different," or "the Realized One exists after death," or "the Realized One does not exist after death," or "the Realized One both exists and does not exist after death," or "the Realized One neither exists nor does not exist after death" — this is the extremist view with ten grounds.

#### Explanation of the Wanderings of Craving ^2-17-12-0

##### (1) With respect to what is internal ^2-17-12-1-0

973. Herein, what are the eighteen wanderings of craving with respect to what is internal? There is "I am," there is "I am thus," there is "I am in this way," there is "I am otherwise," there is "I shall be," there is "I shall be thus," there is "I shall be in this way," there is "I shall be otherwise," there is "may I be," there is "may I be pleasant," there is "may it be," there is "may it be thus," there is "may it be in this way," there is "may it be otherwise," there is "may I not be," there is "may I not be thus," there is "may I not be in this way," there is "may I not be otherwise." ^2-973

974. And how is there "I am"? Having taken no phenomenon as insignificant, one gains desire with regard to material form... feeling... perception... formations... consciousness, thinking "I am"; one gains conceit thinking "I am"; one gains a view thinking "I am." When this is present, these proliferations occur: "I am thus," or "I am in this way," or "I am otherwise."
(2) And how is there "I am thus"? "I am a warrior," or "I am a brahmin," or "I am a merchant," or "I am a laborer," or "I am a layperson," or "I am one gone forth," or "I am a deity," or "I am a human being," or "I am possessed of material form," or "I am immaterial," or "I am percipient," or "I am non-percipient," or "I am neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "I am thus."
(3) And how is there "I am in this way"? Comparing oneself with another person: "as that one is a warrior, so am I a warrior," or "as that one is a brahmin, so am I a brahmin," or "as that one is a merchant, so am I a merchant," or "as that one is a laborer, so am I a laborer," or "as that one is a layperson, so am I a layperson," or "as that one is one gone forth, so am I one gone forth," or "as that one is a deity, so am I a deity," or "as that one is a human being, so am I a human being," or "as that one is possessed of material form, so am I possessed of material form," or "as that one is immaterial, so am I immaterial," or "as that one is percipient, so am I percipient," or "as that one is non-percipient, so am I non-percipient," or "as that one is neither percipient nor non-percipient, so am I neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "I am in this way."
(4) And how is there "I am otherwise"? Comparing oneself with another person: "as that one is a warrior, I am not thus a warrior," or "as that one is a brahmin, I am not thus a brahmin," or "as that one is a merchant, I am not thus a merchant," or "as that one is a laborer, I am not thus a laborer," or "as that one is a layperson, I am not thus a layperson," or "as that one is one gone forth, I am not thus one gone forth," or "as that one is a deity, I am not thus a deity," or "as that one is a human being, I am not thus a human being," or "as that one is possessed of material form, I am not thus possessed of material form," or "as that one is immaterial, I am not thus immaterial," or "as that one is percipient, I am not thus percipient," or "as that one is non-percipient, I am not thus non-percipient," or "as that one is neither percipient nor non-percipient, I am not thus neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "I am otherwise."
(5) And how is there "I shall be"? Having taken no phenomenon as insignificant, one gains desire with regard to material form... feeling... perception... formations... consciousness, thinking "I shall be"; one gains conceit thinking "I shall be"; one gains a view thinking "I shall be." When this is present, these proliferations occur: "I shall be thus," or "I shall be in this way," or "I shall be otherwise."
(6) And how is there "I shall be thus"? "I shall be a warrior," or "I shall be a brahmin," or "I shall be a merchant," or "I shall be a laborer," or "I shall be a layperson," or "I shall be one gone forth," or "I shall be a deity," or "I shall be a human being," or "I shall be possessed of material form," or "I shall be immaterial," or "I shall be percipient," or "I shall be non-percipient," or "I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "I shall be thus."
(7) And how is there "I shall be in this way"? Comparing oneself with another person: "as that one is a warrior, so shall I be a warrior," or "as that one is a brahmin, so shall I be a brahmin"... "as that one is neither percipient nor non-percipient, so shall I be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "I shall be in this way."
(8) And how is there "I shall be otherwise"? Comparing oneself with another person: "as that one is a warrior, I shall not thus be a warrior," or "as that one is a brahmin, I shall not thus be a brahmin"... "as that one is neither percipient nor non-percipient, I shall not thus be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "I shall be otherwise."
(9) And how is there "may I be"? Having taken no phenomenon as insignificant, one thinks with regard to material form... feeling... perception... formations... consciousness: "I am permanent, I am stable, I am eternal, I am not subject to change" — thus there is "may I be."
(10) And how is there "may I be pleasant"? Having taken no phenomenon as insignificant, one thinks with regard to material form... feeling... perception... formations... consciousness: "I shall be cut off, I shall be destroyed, I shall not be" — thus there is "may I be pleasant."
(11) And how is there "may it be"? Having taken no phenomenon as insignificant, one gains desire with regard to material form... feeling... perception... formations... consciousness, thinking "may it be"; one gains conceit thinking "may it be"; one gains a view thinking "may it be." When this is present, these proliferations occur: "may it be thus," or "may it be in this way," or "may it be otherwise."
(12) And how is there "may it be thus"? "May I be a warrior," or "may I be a brahmin," or "may I be a merchant," or "may I be a laborer," or "may I be a layperson," or "may I be one gone forth," or "may I be a deity," or "may I be a human being," or "may I be possessed of material form," or "may I be immaterial," or "may I be percipient," or "may I be non-percipient," or "may I be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "may it be thus."
(13) And how is there "may it be in this way"? Comparing oneself with another person: "as that one is a warrior, so may I be a warrior," or "as that one is a brahmin, so may I be a brahmin"... "as that one is neither percipient nor non-percipient, so may I be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "may it be in this way."
(14) And how is there "may it be otherwise"? Comparing oneself with another person: "as that one is a warrior, may I not thus be a warrior," or "as that one is a brahmin, may I not thus be a brahmin"... "as that one is neither percipient nor non-percipient, may I not thus be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "may it be otherwise."
(15) And how is there "may I not be"? Having taken no phenomenon as insignificant, one gains desire with regard to material form... feeling... perception... formations... consciousness, thinking "may I not be"; one gains conceit thinking "may I not be"; one gains a view thinking "may I not be." When this is present, these proliferations occur: "may I not be thus," or "may I not be in this way," or "may I not be otherwise."
(16) And how is there "may I not be thus"? "May I not be a warrior," or "may I not be a brahmin," or "may I not be a merchant," or "may I not be a laborer," or "may I not be a layperson," or "may I not be one gone forth," or "may I not be a deity," or "may I not be a human being," or "may I not be possessed of material form," or "may I not be immaterial," or "may I not be percipient," or "may I not be non-percipient," or "may I not be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "may I not be thus." (17) And how is there "may I not be in this way"? Comparing oneself with another person: "as that one is a warrior, may I not be a warrior in this way," or "as that one is a brahmin, may I not be a brahmin in this way"... "as that one is neither percipient nor non-percipient, may I not be neither percipient nor non-percipient in this way" — thus there is "may I not be in this way."
(18) And how is there "may I not be otherwise"? Comparing oneself with another person: "as that one is a warrior, may I not otherwise be a warrior," or "as that one is a brahmin, may I not otherwise be a brahmin"... (15) And how is there "by means of this may I not be"? Having taken some phenomenon as significant, one gains desire with regard to material form... feeling... perception... formations... consciousness, thinking "by means of this may I not be"; one gains conceit thinking "by means of this may I not be"; one gains a view thinking "by means of this may I not be." When this is present, these proliferations occur: "by means of this may I not be thus," or "by means of this may I not be in this way," or "by means of this may I not be otherwise."
(16) And how is there "by means of this may I not be thus"? "By means of this may I not be a warrior," or "by means of this may I not be a brahmin," or "by means of this may I not be a merchant," or "by means of this may I not be a laborer," or "by means of this may I not be a layperson," or "by means of this may I not be one gone forth," or "by means of this may I not be a deity," or "by means of this may I not be a human being," or "by means of this may I not be possessed of material form," or "by means of this may I not be immaterial," or "by means of this may I not be percipient," or "by means of this may I not be non-percipient," or "by means of this may I not be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "by means of this may I not be thus."
(17) And how is there "by means of this may I not be in this way"? Comparing oneself with another person: "as that one is a warrior, by means of this may I not be a warrior in this way," or "as that one is a brahmin, by means of this may I not be a brahmin in this way"... "as that one is neither percipient nor non-percipient, by means of this may I not be neither percipient nor non-percipient in this way" — thus there is "by means of this may I not be in this way."
(18) And how is there "by means of this may I not be otherwise"? Comparing oneself with another person: "as that one is a warrior, by means of this may I not otherwise be a warrior," or "as that one is a brahmin, by means of this may I not otherwise be a brahmin"... "as that one is neither percipient nor non-percipient, by means of this may I not otherwise be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "by means of this may I not be otherwise."
These are the eighteen wanderings of craving with respect to what is external.
So there are these eighteen wanderings of craving with respect to what is internal, and these eighteen wanderings of craving with respect to what is external; gathering these together and combining them, there are thirty-six wanderings of craving. So there are such thirty-six wanderings of craving with respect to the past, thirty-six with respect to the future, and thirty-six with respect to the present; gathering these together and combining them, there are one hundred and eight wanderings of craving. ^2-976

977. Herein, what are the sixty-two kinds of views spoken by the Blessed One in the explanation in the Brahmajāla? The four doctrines of eternalism, the four doctrines of partial eternalism, the four doctrines about the finite and the infinite, the four doctrines of endless equivocation, the two doctrines of fortuitous origination, the sixteen doctrines of a percipient [self], the eight doctrines of non-perception, the eight doctrines of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the seven doctrines of annihilation, the five doctrines of extinguishing suffering in this very life — these are the sixty-two kinds of views spoken by the Blessed One in the explanation in the Brahmajāla.
The Analysis of Minor Points is finished. ^2-977

979. Herein, what are the five aggregates? The aggregate of material form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, the aggregate of consciousness – these are called "the five aggregates". ^2-979

The eye element, the sight element, the eye-consciousness element, the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, the nose element, the smell element, the nose-consciousness element, the tongue element, the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, the body element, the tangible element, the body-consciousness element, the mind element, the mental-object element, the mind-consciousness element – these are called "the eighteen elements". ^2-981

984. Herein, what are the nine roots? Three wholesome roots, three unwholesome roots, three neutral roots.
Herein, what are the three wholesome roots? Non-greed as a wholesome root, non-hate as a wholesome root, non-delusion as a wholesome root – these are the three wholesome roots.
Herein, what are the three unwholesome roots? Greed as an unwholesome root, hate as an unwholesome root, delusion as an unwholesome root – these are the three unwholesome roots.
Herein, what are the three neutral roots? Non-greed, non-hate, and non-delusion, whether as the result of wholesome states or among neutral functional states – these are the three neutral roots. These are called "the nine roots". ^2-984

At the moment of rebirth in the material-form element, which three kinds of nutriment appear? Contact as nutriment, mental volition as nutriment, consciousness as nutriment – at the moment of rebirth in the material-form element, these three kinds of nutriment appear.

##### The Non-Percipient Gods ^2-18-4-3-0

1017. At the moment of rebirth of the non-percipient gods, how many aggregates appear ... how many minds appear?
At the moment of rebirth of the non-percipient gods, one aggregate appears – the aggregate of material form; two sense-fields appear – the sight sense-field, the mental-object sense-field; two elements appear – the sight element, the mental-object element; one truth appears – the truth of suffering; one faculty appears – the material life faculty. #### The Section Distinguishing the Planes ^2-18-5-0

1020. Sense-sphere phenomena, phenomena not of the sense sphere, fine-material-sphere phenomena, phenomena not of the fine-material sphere, immaterial-sphere phenomena, phenomena not of the immaterial sphere, included phenomena, phenomena not included.
Which phenomena are of the sense sphere? Taking the Avīci hell as the lower limit and including the gods who wield power over others' creations as the upper limit, whatever aggregates, elements, and sense-fields belong to and are included within that interval – material form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness – these phenomena are of the sense sphere.
Which phenomena are not of the sense sphere? Fine-material-sphere phenomena, immaterial-sphere phenomena, and phenomena not included – these phenomena are not of the sense sphere.
Which phenomena are of the fine-material sphere? Taking the Brahmā world as the lower limit and including the Akaniṭṭha gods as the upper limit, whatever mind and mental-factor states belong to and are included within that interval, whether of one who has attained absorption, or has been reborn there, or dwells happily in this very life – these phenomena are of the fine-material sphere.
Which phenomena are not of the fine-material sphere? Sense-sphere phenomena, immaterial-sphere phenomena, and phenomena not included – these phenomena are not of the fine-material sphere.
Which phenomena are of the immaterial sphere? Taking the gods who have reached the base of infinite space as the lower limit and including the gods who have reached the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the upper limit, whatever mind and mental-factor states belong to and are included within that interval, whether of one who has attained absorption, or has been reborn there, or dwells happily in this very life – these phenomena are of the immaterial sphere.
Which phenomena are not of the immaterial sphere? Sense-sphere phenomena, fine-material-sphere phenomena, and phenomena not included – these phenomena are not of the immaterial sphere.
Which phenomena are included? Wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral phenomena subject to mental taints, belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere; the aggregate of material form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, the aggregate of consciousness – these phenomena are included.
Which phenomena are not included? The paths, the fruits of the paths, and the unconditioned element – these phenomena are not included. ^2-1020

#### The Section on Generating Action and the Measure of Life ^2-18-6-0

##### Generating Action ^2-18-6-1-0

1021. As for "gods": there are three kinds of gods – gods by convention, gods by rebirth, and gods by purity.
Gods by convention are: kings, queens, and princes.
Gods by rebirth are: the gods from the Four Great Kings upward.
Gods by purity are: those called arahants.
Having given gifts, undertaken virtue, and performed the observance-day practice, where are people reborn? Having given gifts, undertaken virtue, and performed the observance-day practice, some are reborn in the company of wealthy noble families, some are reborn in the company of wealthy brahmin families, some are reborn in the company of wealthy householder families, some are reborn in the company of the gods of the Four Great Kings, some are reborn in the company of the gods of the Thirty-three, some are reborn in the company of the Yāma gods, some are reborn in the company of the Tusita gods, some are reborn in the company of the gods who delight in their own creations, some are reborn in the company of the gods who wield power over others' creations. ^2-1021

##### Measure of Life ^2-18-6-2-0

1022. What is the measure of life for humans? A hundred years, a little less or a little more. ^2-1022

1023. What is the measure of life for the gods of the Four Great Kings? Fifty human years are a single day and night for the gods of the Four Great Kings. Thirty such nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year. By that reckoning of years, five hundred such divine years is the measure of life for the gods of the Four Great Kings. In terms of the human count, how much is that? Nine million years.
What is the measure of life for the gods of the Thirty-three? A hundred human years is a single day and night for the gods of the Thirty-three. Thirty such nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year. By that reckoning of years, a thousand such divine years is the measure of life for the gods of the Thirty-three. In terms of the human count, how much is that? Thirty-six million years.
What is the measure of life for the Yāma gods? Two hundred human years is a single day and night for the Yāma gods. Thirty such nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year. By that reckoning of years, two thousand such divine years is the measure of life for the Yāma gods. In terms of the human count, how much is that? A hundred and forty-four million years.
What is the measure of life for the Tusita gods? Four hundred human years is a single day and night for the Tusita gods. Thirty such nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year. By that reckoning of years, four thousand such divine years is the measure of life for the Tusita gods. In terms of the human count, how much is that? Five hundred and seventy-six million years.
What is the measure of life for the gods who delight in their own creations? Eight hundred human years is a single day and night for the gods who delight in their own creations. Thirty such nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year. By that reckoning of years, eight thousand such divine years is the measure of life for the gods who delight in their own creations. In terms of the human count, how much is that? Two billion three hundred and four million years.
What is the measure of life for the gods who wield power over others' creations? Sixteen hundred human years is a single day and night for the gods who wield power over others' creations. Thirty such nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year. By that reckoning of years, sixteen thousand such divine years is the measure of life for the gods who wield power over others' creations. In terms of the human count, how much is that? Nine billion two hundred and sixteen million years.
These six belong to the sense sphere, all abounding in every sense pleasure;
reckoned together, what is the sum of their lifespans?
Twelve billion years are theirs, and two hundred eighty million more;
and five million years besides – thus is it declared, reckoned in years. ^2-1023

1024. Having developed the first absorption to a limited degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the first absorption to a limited degree, they are reborn in the company of the Brahmā's-retinue gods. What is the measure of their life? A third of an eon.
Having developed the first absorption to a middling degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the first absorption to a middling degree, they are reborn in the company of the Brahmā's-ministers gods. What is the measure of their life? Half an eon.
Having developed the first absorption to a superior degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the first absorption to a superior degree, they are reborn in the company of the Great Brahmā gods. What is the measure of their life? One eon. ^2-1024

1025. Having developed the second absorption to a limited degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the second absorption to a limited degree, they are reborn in the company of the gods of limited radiance. What is the measure of their life? Two eons.
Having developed the second absorption to a middling degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the second absorption to a middling degree, they are reborn in the company of the gods of unbounded radiance. What is the measure of their life? Four eons.
Having developed the second absorption to a superior degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the second absorption to a superior degree, they are reborn in the company of the gods of streaming radiance. What is the measure of their life? Eight eons. ^2-1025

1026. Having developed the third absorption to a limited degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the third absorption to a limited degree, they are reborn in the company of the gods of limited glory. What is the measure of their life? Sixteen eons.
Having developed the third absorption to a middling degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the third absorption to a middling degree, they are reborn in the company of the gods of unbounded glory. What is the measure of their life? Thirty-two eons.
Having developed the third absorption to a superior degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the third absorption to a superior degree, they are reborn in the company of the gods of refulgent glory. What is the measure of their life? Sixty-four eons. ^2-1026

1027. Having developed the fourth absorption, owing to differences in the object, differences in attention, differences in intention, differences in aspiration, differences in resolution, differences in application, and differences in wisdom, some are reborn in the company of the non-percipient gods, some are reborn in the company of the Vehapphala gods, some are reborn in the company of the Aviha gods, some are reborn in the company of the Atappa gods, some are reborn in the company of the Sudassa gods, some are reborn in the company of the Sudassī gods, some are reborn in the company of the Akaniṭṭha gods, some are reborn in the company of the gods who have reached the base of infinite space, some are reborn in the company of the gods who have reached the base of infinite consciousness, some are reborn in the company of the gods who have reached the base of nothingness, some are reborn in the company of the gods who have reached the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What is the measure of life for the non-percipient gods and the Vehapphala gods? Five hundred eons.
What is the measure of life for the Aviha gods? A thousand eons.
What is the measure of life for the Atappa gods? Two thousand eons.
What is the measure of life for the Sudassa gods? Four thousand eons.
What is the measure of life for the Sudassī gods? Eight thousand eons.
What is the measure of life for the Akaniṭṭha gods? Sixteen thousand eons. ^2-1027

1028. What is the measure of life for the gods who have reached the base of infinite space? Twenty thousand eons.
What is the measure of life for the gods who have reached the base of infinite consciousness? Forty thousand eons.
What is the measure of life for the gods who have reached the base of nothingness? Sixty thousand eons.
What is the measure of life for the gods who have reached the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception? Eighty-four thousand eons. ^2-1028

1029. Lifted up by the power of merit, they go to a destination in the sense sphere or the fine-material sphere;
even having reached the peak of existence, they come again to a bad destination.
Beings so long-lived nevertheless pass away when their lifespan is exhausted;
there is no state of existence that is permanent — so it was said by the great sage.
Therefore the wise, the prudent, the skillful, who reflect on what is truly beneficial,
develop the supreme path for release from aging and death.
Having developed the pure path that leads down into Nibbāna,
having fully understood all mental taints, they attain final Nibbāna free of taints. ^2-1029

#### The Section on What Is to Be Directly Known, and So On ^2-18-7-0

1030. Of the five aggregates, how many are to be directly known, how many are to be fully understood, how many are to be abandoned, how many are to be developed, how many are to be realized, how many are neither to be abandoned, nor to be developed, nor to be realized ... of the seven minds, how many are to be directly known, how many are to be fully understood, how many are to be abandoned, how many are to be developed, how many are to be realized, how many are neither to be abandoned, nor to be developed, nor to be realized? ^2-1030

1031. The aggregate of material form is to be directly known and to be fully understood, but is not to be abandoned, not to be developed, not to be realized. The four other aggregates are to be directly known and to be fully understood; they may be to be abandoned, may be to be developed, may be to be realized, may be neither to be abandoned, nor to be developed, nor to be realized.
Ten sense-fields are to be directly known and to be fully understood, but are not to be abandoned, not to be developed, not to be realized. The two other sense-fields are to be directly known and to be fully understood; they may be to be abandoned, may be to be developed, may be to be realized, may be neither to be abandoned, nor to be developed, nor to be realized.
Sixteen elements are to be directly known and to be fully understood, but are not to be abandoned, not to be developed, not to be realized. The two other elements are to be directly known and to be fully understood; they may be to be abandoned, may be to be developed, may be to be realized, may be neither to be abandoned, nor to be developed, nor to be realized.
The truth of the origin is to be directly known, to be fully understood, and to be abandoned, but is not to be developed, not to be realized. The truth of the path is to be directly known and to be fully understood, and is to be developed, but is not to be abandoned, not to be realized. The truth of the cessation is to be directly known and to be fully understood, and is to be realized, but is not to be abandoned, not to be developed. The truth of suffering is to be directly known and to be fully understood; it may be to be abandoned, is not to be developed, is not to be realized, and it may be not to be abandoned.
Nine faculties are to be directly known and to be fully understood, but are not to be abandoned, not to be developed, not to be realized. The faculty of displeasure is to be directly known, to be fully understood, and to be abandoned, but is not to be developed, not to be realized. The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" is to be directly known and to be fully understood, and is to be developed, but is not to be abandoned, not to be realized. The faculty of full knowledge is to be directly known and to be fully understood, is not to be abandoned; it may be to be developed, may be to be realized. The faculty of one who has fully known is to be directly known and to be fully understood, and is to be realized, but is not to be abandoned, not to be developed. The three remaining faculties are to be directly known and to be fully understood, are not to be abandoned; they may be to be developed, may be to be realized, may be not to be developed but to be realized. The six other faculties are to be directly known and to be fully understood; they may be to be abandoned, may be to be developed, may be to be realized, may be neither to be abandoned, nor to be developed, nor to be realized.
The three unwholesome roots are to be directly known, to be fully understood, and to be abandoned, but are not to be developed, not to be realized. The three wholesome roots are to be directly known and to be fully understood, are not to be abandoned; they may be to be developed, are not to be realized, and may be not to be developed. The three neutral roots are to be directly known and to be fully understood, are not to be abandoned, not to be developed; they may be to be realized, may be not to be realized.

##### (2) The Worldly/World-Transcending Pair ^2-18-10-7-0

1044. Of the five aggregates, how many are worldly, how many are world-transcending? Of the twelve sense-fields, how many are worldly, how many are world-transcending? Six perceptions are worldly. Perception born of mind-consciousness-element contact may be worldly, may be world-transcending. Six intentions are worldly. Intention born of mind-consciousness-element contact may be worldly, may be world-transcending. Six minds are worldly. The mind-consciousness element may be worldly, may be world-transcending.
Direct knowledge, the two having-an-object sections, the seen, the wholesome, feeling;
the resultant, the clung-to, applied thought, the material, and the worldly – thus are they told.
The Analysis of the Heart of Phenomena is finished.
The Book of Analysis is finished. ^2-1044
